lessonTitle: What is TOGAF — and What Problem Does It Solve?
sourceRef: C220Part0e §1.1 — "What is an Enterprise?"
scenario: Three independent hospitals, each with its own board and separate ownership, are forming a shared clinical data consortium — no merger, no shared parent company, just a formal agreement to jointly fund a common patient-referral platform. The consortium's newly appointed lead architect is told by a hospital board member: "You can't really do 'Enterprise Architecture' here — we're three separate legal entities, not one company. There's no single enterprise to architect."

options.action: Agree — Enterprise Architecture requires a single legal entity or corporate parent; recommend each hospital instead develop its own separate architecture and coordinate informally.
options.rationale: Directly contradicts the Standard's definition. "Enterprise" explicitly does not require single ownership — a consortium of independent organizations working toward common goals is one of the Standard's own named examples of a valid enterprise.

options.action: Disagree — explain that TOGAF's definition of "enterprise" is broader than a single company, and note that partnerships and alliances can qualify.
options.rationale: Correct in substance but incomplete — doesn't anchor the response in the Standard's specific language or give the board member a citable definition, leaving the claim easy to dismiss as the architect's personal opinion rather than the Standard's own position.

options.action: Disagree, citing the Standard directly: "an enterprise" is defined as any collection of organizations with common goals — explicitly including "partnerships and alliances of businesses working together, such as a consortium." The three hospitals jointly funding a shared platform are exactly this kind of enterprise, regardless of separate legal ownership.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly applies the Standard's actual definition and its specific named example (consortium), directly rebutting the board member's premise with citable authority rather than general reassurance.

options.action: Agree that a single "enterprise" doesn't exist yet, and propose the three hospitals first merge governance structures before any Enterprise Architecture work begins.
options.rationale: Unnecessary and contradicts the Standard — merging governance is not a prerequisite for Enterprise Architecture; the three-hospital consortium already qualifies as an enterprise as described, without requiring structural unification first.

lessonTitle: What is TOGAF — and What Problem Does It Solve?
sourceRef: C220Part0e §2.2 — TOGAF Documentation Set, selective adoption guidance
scenario: A mid-size logistics firm is adopting TOGAF for the first time. The newly hired Enterprise Architect proposes: "We'll fully implement all six TOGAF documents simultaneously — Introduction and Core Concepts, ADM, ADM Techniques, Applying the ADM, Architecture Content, and EA Capability and Governance — from day one, so we get the complete framework properly." The CIO, who has read a TOGAF overview, pushes back.

options.action: Support the architect's plan — TOGAF's six documents form an indivisible whole and must be adopted together to be standards-compliant.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard directly. It explicitly states organizations may adopt the ADM process while electing not to use materials relating to Architecture Capability, and that incremental adoption of particular constituent documents is expected and encouraged.

options.action: Side with the CIO's instinct that this is too much at once, and suggest picking "whichever document seems most urgent" without a structured rationale.
options.rationale: Directionally right but underspecified — correctly senses that selective adoption is valid but doesn't ground the recommendation in the Standard's actual guidance about how organizations new to TOGAF are expected to approach adoption.

options.action: Advise that the Standard explicitly anticipates this situation: organizations new to TOGAF are expected to focus on particular constituent documents for initial adoption, tabling others for later. Recommend starting with the ADM (the core method) and Introduction and Core Concepts, deferring EA Capability and Governance and the other documents until the organization has direct experience to tailor them against.
options.rationale: Best answer — cites the Standard's specific guidance for organizations new to TOGAF, and proposes a concrete, staged adoption sequence consistent with that guidance rather than an all-at-once or arbitrary approach.

options.action: Recommend adopting only the ADM document and permanently excluding the other five, since the ADM is the core of TOGAF and the rest is optional extra material.
options.rationale: Overcorrects — the Standard frames the other five documents as available for adoption over time, not permanently irrelevant; "tabled for later consideration" is different from permanent exclusion, especially once the organization has built experience with the ADM.

lessonTitle: What is TOGAF — and What Problem Does It Solve?
scenario: A retail chain's newly formed architecture team is under pressure to "show progress fast." The team lead proposes starting immediately with Technology Architecture — selecting a new cloud platform and finalising vendor contracts in the first month — arguing that "the business side can catch up once the technical foundation is locked in."

options.action: Support starting with Technology Architecture, since infrastructure decisions take the longest lead time and should be secured first.
options.rationale: Inverts the BDAT dependency chain the lesson establishes. Technology exists to serve business and data needs — locking in infrastructure before those needs are understood risks building the wrong platform for requirements that haven't yet been defined.

options.action: Push back only on the vendor contract timing, but agree that starting with Technology Architecture generally is fine as long as contracts aren't finalised yet.
options.rationale: Addresses a symptom (contract timing) without addressing the underlying sequencing problem — starting analysis at Technology Architecture, contracts aside, still risks technology-driven rather than business-driven design.

options.action: Push back on the sequencing itself: recommend Business Architecture first, to establish what the retail chain actually needs to achieve, before Data, Application, and only then Technology decisions are made — explaining that BDAT's order reflects a genuine dependency, not an arbitrary convention.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly identifies that the BDAT order (Business → Data → Application → Technology) exists because each layer depends on the one before it, and that skipping to Technology first inverts this dependency regardless of time pressure.

options.action: Suggest running Business Architecture and Technology Architecture analysis in parallel to save time, with the two teams reconciling findings at the end.
options.rationale: Shows awareness that Business Architecture matters but underestimates the dependency — Technology Architecture decisions made in parallel, before Business Architecture concludes, risk being based on requirements that later change once the Business Architecture work is actually complete.

lessonTitle: What is TOGAF — and What Problem Does It Solve?
scenario: An architect produces a single diagram showing the target-state system landscape for a new claims-processing platform and presents it to the steering committee as "the architecture." A committee member later asks: "Where are the principles and rules that will govern how this system evolves once it's live? Isn't that supposed to be part of the architecture too?"

options.action: Explain that principles and governance rules are a separate, unrelated exercise from architecture, to be handled by IT operations after go-live.
options.rationale: Contradicts the lesson's core distinction. TOGAF defines "architecture" as having two meanings — one of which is precisely the structure of components together with the principles and guidelines governing their design and evolution. Treating governance as unrelated misses half the definition.

options.action: Agree the diagram was incomplete, and offer to add a short appendix listing a few general best-practice guidelines.
options.rationale: Moves in the right direction by acknowledging the gap, but "a few general best-practice guidelines" undersells what's needed — the second meaning of architecture calls for genuine governing principles tied to this system's design and evolution, not generic best practices.

options.action: Acknowledge the committee member is right: the diagram only captured one of TOGAF's two meanings of "architecture" — the formal description/plan. The second meaning — the structure of components plus the principles and guidelines governing their design and evolution — still needs to be documented, and commit to producing it before the architecture is considered complete.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly identifies which of the two official meanings was covered (the plan) and which was missing (the governing principles), and treats both as necessary rather than optional add-ons.

options.action: Defend the diagram as sufficient, since TOGAF's Architecture Vision is meant to be high-level and doesn't require governance detail at this stage.
options.rationale: Misapplies a different concept — the Architecture Vision being appropriately high-level (a Phase A characteristic) doesn't answer the committee member's more fundamental question about whether governing principles are part of "architecture" as a concept at all, which they are, per the Standard's own two-part definition.

lessonTitle: The TOGAF Documentation Set
sourceRef: C220Part0e §2.2, Figure 2-3 — TOGAF Standard structure (Fundamental Content vs Series Guides)
scenario: An architecture team preparing a compliance report writes: "Our organization has fully adopted the TOGAF Standard, including all TOGAF Series Guides such as Business Architecture, Security Architecture, and Enterprise Architecture/Agile Architecture." A reviewing auditor questions whether this claim is even a coherent thing to assert.

options.action: Confirm the claim is coherent and accurate — the Series Guides are simply an extension of the six Fundamental Content documents, and "full adoption" of the Standard naturally includes all of them.
options.rationale: Wrong. The Standard explicitly notes that not all TOGAF Series Guides will be relevant in every situation — they exist to address specific concerns and use cases, not as a mandatory checklist to be fully adopted alongside the six Fundamental Content documents.

options.action: Flag that the claim seems too broad, and suggest the team specify which Series Guides are actually relevant to their context.
options.rationale: Correct instinct but doesn't explain why the original claim was structurally wrong — doesn't distinguish between the six Fundamental Content documents (the core Standard) and the Series Guides (supplementary, situational) as two distinct structural elements.

options.action: Explain that the TOGAF Standard is structured as two distinct parts: the six free-standing Fundamental Content documents (the core, generally applicable to any adoption) and the separate TOGAF Series Guides (supplementary material addressing specific concerns, of which "not all... will be relevant in every situation"). "Full adoption of all Series Guides" isn't a meaningful or expected claim — the team should instead report which Fundamental Content documents they use and which specific Series Guides are relevant to their context.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly separates the two structural elements of the Standard and directly cites the guidance that Series Guide relevance is situational, not something to be exhaustively "fully adopted."

options.action: Reject the claim entirely and recommend the team state they have adopted none of the Series Guides, only the six core documents.
options.rationale: Overcorrects — the Standard doesn't discourage using Series Guides; it simply notes their relevance is situational. A team legitimately using specific Series Guides relevant to their context (e.g., Security Architecture) should say so, not claim to use none.

lessonTitle: The TOGAF Documentation Set
sourceRef: C220Part0e §2.2 — six Fundamental Content documents, listed in order
scenario: During an internal training session, a junior architect lists what she believes are the six TOGAF Fundamental Content documents: Introduction and Core Concepts, Architecture Development Method, ADM Techniques, Architecture Content, Enterprise Architecture Capability and Governance, and TOGAF Series Guides. A colleague says this list looks slightly off.

options.action: Confirm the list is correct as stated — all six items are legitimately part of the TOGAF Standard's structure.
options.rationale: Wrong. While all six items she named do relate to TOGAF, "TOGAF Series Guides" is not one of the six Fundamental Content documents — it's a separate collection of guidance material sitting alongside the six documents, and she has also omitted "Applying the ADM" from her list entirely.

options.action: Point out that TOGAF Series Guides shouldn't be counted as one of the six, but don't identify what document is actually missing from her list.
options.rationale: Correctly identifies half the problem (Series Guides isn't one of the six) but leaves the correction incomplete — a fully correct answer needs to also name the missing sixth document.

options.action: Correct the list precisely: the sixth Fundamental Content document she's missing is "Applying the ADM" (guidelines for adapting the ADM to specific practical contexts) — and "TOGAF Series Guides" should be removed from the list, since it's a separate supplementary collection, not one of the six Fundamental Content documents itself.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly identifies both errors: the missing document (Applying the ADM) and the incorrectly included item (Series Guides), restoring the accurate six-document list.

options.action: Tell her the exact list doesn't matter much, since all TOGAF documentation works together as a whole regardless of how it's categorized.
options.rationale: Dismisses a legitimate factual correction. While the documents do work together, knowing precisely which six documents constitute the Fundamental Content — and that Series Guides are structurally separate — is exam-relevant and professionally relevant, not a detail to wave away.

lessonTitle: The TOGAF Documentation Set
scenario: A consultancy pitches a client: "We'll implement TOGAF's ADM exactly as documented, with zero customisation — this guarantees the most 'pure' and defensible architecture outcome." The client's CIO, who has done some independent reading, asks whether that's really how TOGAF is meant to be used.

options.action: Confirm the consultancy's pitch — following the ADM exactly as documented, without adaptation, is indeed the TOGAF-recommended approach and the safest way to guarantee compliance.
options.rationale: Contradicts a core theme of the lesson. TOGAF is explicitly a foundational framework meant to be adapted to context — zero customisation is not the recommended posture, and treating rigid literal application as "most defensible" misunderstands how the Standard is intended to be used.

options.action: Note that some adaptation is normal, but suggest the client not worry about the specifics since "most organisations customise it a little."
options.rationale: Points in the right direction but is vague — doesn't explain that TOGAF explicitly anticipates adaptation as part of its design, or point to the kinds of adaptation guidance that exist to support this properly.

options.action: Explain that TOGAF is designed as a foundational framework applicable to any context, and adaptation is expected, not a deviation from best practice — the deliverables and artifacts described in the ADM phases are meant to be adapted to reflect the specific needs of the enterprise, with further guidance available through the TOGAF Standard — Architecture Content and relevant Series Guides.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly frames adaptation as the intended mode of use for a foundational framework, not an exception, and points to where more specific adaptation guidance can be found.

options.action: Suggest the client insist on zero customisation for the first year, then begin adapting the ADM in year two once the team has more experience.
options.rationale: Introduces an arbitrary timeline not supported by the lesson's content — there's no basis for a mandatory 'customisation-free' first year; adaptation to the enterprise's specific needs is appropriate from the outset, proportionate to context.

lessonTitle: The TOGAF Documentation Set
scenario: A large enterprise already has a mature, home-grown architecture framework with its own well-established documentation, tools, and stakeholder buy-in built over a decade. A newly hired Chief Architect proposes: "We should discard our existing framework entirely and replace it wholesale with an unmodified TOGAF implementation, since TOGAF is the industry-recognised standard."

options.action: Support the wholesale replacement — since TOGAF is the recognised industry standard, any existing home-grown framework should be fully discarded in its favour.
options.rationale: Wrong. The lesson explicitly notes that organizations with already-deployed architecture frameworks may choose to merge those frameworks with aspects of the TOGAF Standard — wholesale discarding an established, working framework is not the only or necessarily the best path.

options.action: Recommend keeping the existing framework entirely unchanged and only referencing TOGAF informally for terminology.
options.rationale: Swings too far the other way — underuses TOGAF's genuine value (a common method and vocabulary) when there may be real benefit in merging specific TOGAF elements with the existing framework, rather than treating TOGAF as merely a glossary to consult informally.

options.action: Recommend a merge approach: retain the elements of the existing framework that already work and have stakeholder buy-in, while selectively introducing specific TOGAF elements — such as the ADM's phase structure or the Architecture Content Framework — where they add clear value, consistent with the Standard's own guidance that organizations with existing frameworks may merge them with aspects of TOGAF.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly applies the Standard's explicit guidance for organizations with existing frameworks, proposing selective integration rather than either wholesale replacement or ignoring TOGAF's value entirely.

options.action: Recommend running both frameworks fully and independently in parallel indefinitely, letting teams choose which one to follow for each project.
options.rationale: Creates unnecessary confusion and duplication — running two full, independent frameworks in parallel indefinitely is neither what the Standard's merge guidance suggests nor a practical governance outcome; a deliberate, integrated approach is preferable to indefinite parallel frameworks.

lessonTitle: The Four Architecture Domains (BDAT)
sourceRef: C220-Part1e §5.2 — Phase C Approach (Data vs Application sequencing)
scenario: Two senior architects on the same programme disagree publicly in a planning meeting. Architect A insists: "We must do Data Architecture before Application Architecture — that's the only correct TOGAF sequence, full stop." Architect B insists the opposite: "No, Application Architecture must come first — ERP systems like ours are application-centric, so anything else is wrong." The programme sponsor asks you, as the lead architect, to settle the dispute.

options.action: Side fully with Architect A — Data Architecture must always precede Application Architecture, since data is the more fundamental concern.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard directly. Phase C explicitly involves "some combination of Data and Application Architecture, in either order," with advocates existing for both sequences — there is no single mandated order.

options.action: Side fully with Architect B — Application Architecture must always precede Data Architecture for ERP-centric programmes, since applications like ERP and CRM combine business logic with infrastructure.
options.rationale: Also contradicts the Standard. While ERP/CRM-centric programmes are a legitimate case for an application-driven approach, the Standard doesn't mandate this as the universal rule either — it presents both approaches as valid depending on context.

options.action: Explain that the Standard explicitly supports both sequences: a data-driven approach (referencing methods like Spewak's Enterprise Architecture Planning) and an application-driven approach (common where core systems like ERP or CRM combine business logic and infrastructure). Ask both architects what specifically makes their programme's context better suited to one order over the other, rather than treating it as a universal rule.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly identifies that TOGAF supports both orderings by design, cites the two named approaches from the Standard, and redirects the debate toward the actual decision criterion: programme context, not dogma.

options.action: Tell both architects the order doesn't matter at all and instruct them to run Data and Application Architecture completely simultaneously with no coordination between the two workstreams.
options.rationale: Overcorrects into a different mistake — while TOGAF doesn't mandate a fixed order, that doesn't mean the two workstreams should proceed with zero coordination; some sequencing logic or dependency management between them is still sensible even when either order is valid.

lessonTitle: The Four Architecture Domains (BDAT)
sourceRef: C220-Part1e §6.5.1 — Data Architecture: four types of data
scenario: A Data Architect is asked by the compliance team to produce a complete Data Architecture that addresses "everything the regulator will ask about." She produces a model covering database schemas and API payloads only, and declares it complete. A colleague reviewing her work asks whether two categories have been missed — one covering information shown directly to end users in application screens, and one covering the organization's legally required public data disclosures.

options.action: Confirm her model is complete — database schemas (data at rest) and API payloads (data in motion) are the only two data types TOGAF's Data Architecture needs to address.
options.rationale: Wrong. The Standard identifies four types of data a Data Architecture should handle: data at rest, data in motion, data in use (at the application border, e.g., the GUI), and open data (public disclosures). Only addressing two of the four leaves real regulatory gaps, especially for public data obligations.

options.action: Agree something is missing and suggest she add a section on "user interface data" without mentioning the public-disclosure category at all.
options.rationale: Catches one of the two missing categories (data in use) but misses the other (open data) — for a compliance-driven review specifically, omitting legally required public disclosures is a significant gap to leave unaddressed.

options.action: Point out that her model is missing two of the Standard's four recognized data types: data in use (data at the border of the application, such as the GUI) and open data (data the organization provides for public usage, voluntarily or as a legal requirement) — both directly relevant to a compliance-focused review, since public disclosure obligations fall squarely under open data.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly identifies both missing categories by name and explains why the omission specifically matters for a compliance context, since open data covers exactly the kind of regulatory disclosure being asked about.

options.action: Suggest her model is fine as a starting point, and that data in use and open data can be addressed later during Phase D once the Technology Architecture is defined.
options.rationale: Misplaces the responsibility — data in use and open data are Data Architecture concerns addressed in Phase C, not Technology Architecture concerns deferred to Phase D. Postponing them changes which phase and which domain is responsible for the gap.

lessonTitle: The Four Architecture Domains (BDAT)
scenario: A CTO tells the architecture team: "We don't need a separate Security Architecture team — TOGAF doesn't have a fifth domain for it, so let's just fold security into whichever domain team feels like handling it on a given project, informally."

options.action: Agree — since there's no fifth domain, security can be handled ad hoc by whichever team happens to pick it up on a given project.
options.rationale: Half right, half wrong. Correctly notes there's no fifth domain, but wrongly concludes this means security should be handled informally and inconsistently — the lesson's point is that security is addressed by deliberately combining views across all four domains, not by leaving it to chance.

options.action: Disagree, and propose creating a formal fifth "Security Architecture" domain alongside Business, Data, Application, and Technology.
options.rationale: Overcorrects in the wrong direction — TOGAF explicitly does not add a fifth domain for concerns like security; instead, such cross-cutting concerns are addressed by combining views across the four existing domains, not by inventing a new one.

options.action: Disagree with the "informal, whoever feels like it" approach — confirm there's no fifth domain, but explain that security should be addressed deliberately by combining relevant views across all four domains (e.g., a security view of the data model, a security view of the application interactions, a security view of the technology infrastructure), coordinated rather than left to chance.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly applies the lesson's core point: no fifth domain exists, but that means security requires deliberate, coordinated cross-domain view-building, not the absence of any structured ownership at all.

options.action: Suggest security should be added as a new step within Phase A only, since that's where stakeholder concerns are first identified.
options.rationale: Too narrow — treating security as a one-time Phase A activity misses that it needs to be addressed consistently across Business, Data, Application, and Technology domains throughout the ADM, not resolved once at the start and left alone afterward.

lessonTitle: The Four Architecture Domains (BDAT)
scenario: A programme manager, under deadline pressure, proposes: "Let's skip Business Architecture entirely for this project — we already know what technology we're buying (a specific CRM platform), so let's start directly with Technology Architecture and work backward from there to figure out the business processes afterward."

options.action: Agree — since the technology choice is already made, starting with Technology Architecture and inferring business processes afterward is an efficient shortcut.
options.rationale: Inverts the BDAT dependency entirely. Business Architecture exists to define what the enterprise needs to achieve; deriving business processes backward from a pre-selected technology risks fitting the business to the tool rather than the tool to genuine business needs.

options.action: Disagree, but only suggest running a brief one-day workshop to "rubber-stamp" the existing plan with some business terminology added after the fact.
options.rationale: Acknowledges a problem but doesn't actually fix the sequencing issue — a token workshop to add business language onto an already-decided technology plan doesn't provide the substantive Business Architecture that should inform, not follow, technology choices.

options.action: Disagree, and explain that even where a technology platform is already selected, Business Architecture should still define the target business processes and capabilities the CRM must support — this determines configuration, customisation, and integration priorities, and may reveal the pre-selected platform doesn't fully fit actual business needs, which is better discovered now than after implementation.
options.rationale: Best answer — maintains the correct BDAT dependency logic even in a case where a technology decision has seemingly already been made, and identifies the real risk of skipping Business Architecture: discovering platform-business misalignment only after go-live.

options.action: Suggest abandoning the CRM platform choice entirely and restarting the technology selection process from scratch before doing any Business Architecture work.
options.rationale: Disproportionate — the issue isn't necessarily that the technology choice is wrong, but that Business Architecture work needs to happen to validate and inform how that technology is configured and used; discarding the platform decision outright isn't a justified conclusion at this stage.

lessonTitle: Deliverables, Artifacts, and Building Blocks
sourceRef: C220Part0e §3.6 / C220-Part4e §1.1 — ABB/SBB definitions and satellite network example
scenario: An enterprise defines a requirement: "Field offices in remote regions need a reliable network connection." Region A implements this using a satellite hive of many microsatellites. Region B implements the same requirement using a small set of large satellites instead. A newly hired architect flags this as an inconsistency: "We can't have two different network solutions for the same requirement — one of these regions must be non-compliant."

options.action: Agree with the new architect — since the two regions used different satellite configurations, one of them must be violating the architecture and needs to be corrected to match the other.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard's own example almost exactly. The Standard specifically illustrates that a network is an ABB that can be realized by different SBB implementation choices — such as a satellite network in two major configurations: a hive of microsatellites or a small set of large satellites — treating both as valid, not as a compliance problem.

options.action: Disagree, and explain generally that different regions are allowed to make different technology choices without further clarifying why in ABB/SBB terms.
options.rationale: Reaches the right conclusion but doesn't use the precise vocabulary or reasoning — a stronger answer explicitly identifies which is the ABB (the required network capability) and which are the SBBs (the two different satellite configurations) to make the distinction clear and defensible.

options.action: Disagree, and clarify using ABB/SBB terms: the reliable network connection is the Architecture Building Block — the required capability, described independent of implementation. Each region's specific satellite configuration is a Solution Building Block — an actual implementation choice realizing that capability. Both regions satisfy the same ABB using different, equally valid SBBs; this is expected, not a compliance failure.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly and precisely applies the ABB/SBB distinction to explain why two different implementations of the same requirement are both valid, directly mirroring the Standard's own illustrative example.

options.action: Suggest resolving the disagreement by having both regions abandon their current satellite approaches and switch to a completely new, third technology instead.
options.rationale: Unnecessary and disruptive — there's no actual problem to resolve here; both existing implementations are valid ways of realizing the same ABB, so scrapping both in favor of a third option solves a problem that doesn't exist.

lessonTitle: Deliverables, Artifacts, and Building Blocks
sourceRef: C220Part0e §3.6 — "An artifact may or may not be considered a deliverable based on the contractual specification"
scenario: A project team produces an Application Interaction Matrix showing how their new systems will communicate. The Programme Director asks: "Is this matrix a deliverable? I need to know whether it has to be formally signed off by the steering committee or not." The team lead responds: "All artifacts are deliverables — anything we produce during architecture work has to be formally signed off."

options.action: Confirm the team lead's statement — all artifacts are, by definition, deliverables requiring formal sign-off.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard directly. It explicitly states that "an artifact may or may not be considered a deliverable based on the contractual specification" — meaning whether an artifact requires formal sign-off depends on what was contractually agreed, not on the fact that it's an artifact.

options.action: Disagree with the team lead, but tell the Programme Director that no artifacts require formal sign-off — only formally named deliverables like the Architecture Definition Document ever need approval.
options.rationale: Overcorrects — while it's true not all artifacts require sign-off, this framing wrongly implies artifacts can never be treated as deliverables. In practice, some individual artifacts CAN be contractually specified as deliverables requiring their own sign-off, depending on what was agreed for this engagement.

options.action: Correct the team lead: whether the Application Interaction Matrix is a deliverable requiring formal sign-off depends on the contractual specification for this engagement — check the Statement of Architecture Work or equivalent agreement to see if this specific artifact was named as a required, sign-off deliverable, rather than assuming either way by default.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly applies the Standard's own qualifier ("based on the contractual specification") rather than treating either "all artifacts are deliverables" or "no artifacts are deliverables" as a universal rule.

options.action: Tell the Programme Director this distinction doesn't really matter in practice and any artifact can be treated informally regardless of what was contractually specified.
options.rationale: Dismisses a distinction the Standard treats as meaningful — whether something is contractually specified as requiring formal sign-off has real governance consequences, and isn't something to wave away as unimportant.

lessonTitle: Deliverables, Artifacts, and Building Blocks
scenario: An architect is asked to produce an ABB for a new "Customer Identity Verification" capability. She writes: "This capability will be implemented using Okta's identity verification API, configured with a 3-factor authentication flow and a 200ms response time SLA." A colleague reviewing the document says something about this doesn't look right for an ABB.

options.action: Confirm the document is a correctly written ABB, since it clearly describes what the identity verification capability needs to do.
options.rationale: Wrong — despite describing a capability, the document names a specific vendor product (Okta) and its API, which makes this a Solution Building Block description, not an Architecture Building Block. ABBs describe required capability independent of implementation choice.

options.action: Point out that the document is actually an SBB, without explaining what a properly written ABB version would look like instead.
options.rationale: Correctly identifies the core problem but leaves the fix incomplete — a stronger answer would also show what the corresponding ABB should contain, to make the distinction actionable rather than just diagnostic.

options.action: Point out that this document actually describes a Solution Building Block, not an ABB — it names a specific vendor (Okta) and specific implementation details. A proper ABB would instead describe the required capability independent of implementation: e.g., "Customer Identity Verification capability: must support multi-factor authentication and respond within 200ms," leaving the vendor and specific API choice to be decided separately as the SBB.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly identifies the vendor-specific content as the SBB-level detail, and shows precisely how to rewrite the same requirement at the proper ABB level, preserving the performance requirement while removing the implementation commitment.

options.action: Suggest the document is fine as written, but recommend also producing a second, separate ABB for a backup vendor in case Okta becomes unavailable.
options.rationale: Misses the actual problem — the issue isn't that only one vendor option was documented; it's that the document conflates the ABB (capability) and SBB (implementation) levels entirely. Adding a second vendor-specific document doesn't fix the categorization error, it just repeats it.

lessonTitle: Deliverables, Artifacts, and Building Blocks
scenario: A junior architect produces a single-page list titled "All Applications in the Enterprise," showing application names and their business owners. His manager reviews it and says: "This isn't really an artifact in the TOGAF sense — it's just an informal reference document."

options.action: Agree with the manager — an informal list like this doesn't count as a proper TOGAF artifact since it wasn't produced using specialist modeling tools.
options.rationale: Wrong. Artifacts are classified simply by what they show — catalogs are lists of things, matrices show relationships, diagrams are pictures. A list of applications with their owners is a catalog by definition, regardless of whether it was produced with specialist tooling or a simple document.

options.action: Disagree with the manager and say it's a valid artifact, without identifying which of the three artifact types it actually is.
options.rationale: Reaches the correct conclusion but is incomplete — properly classifying the artifact (as a catalog specifically, not a matrix or diagram) demonstrates the reasoning rather than just asserting a conclusion.

options.action: Disagree with the manager: this is a valid artifact — specifically a catalog, since it's a list of one type of building block (applications) used for reference and governance purposes. It doesn't need specialist tooling or complex formatting to qualify; it just needs to list building blocks of a specific type, which this does.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly classifies the artifact as a catalog by applying the actual defining test (a list of one type of thing) rather than an irrelevant test like tool sophistication or document formality.

options.action: Suggest the list should be converted into a diagram before it can be considered a genuine artifact.
options.rationale: Introduces an unnecessary and incorrect requirement — a list of applications is already a legitimate artifact type (a catalog) on its own; converting it to a diagram doesn't make it "more of an artifact," it just produces a different artifact type serving a different purpose.

lessonTitle: Architecture Principles — The Rules That Govern Everything
sourceRef: C220Part2e §2.3 — Recommended Format for Defining Principles (Name/Statement guidance)
scenario: An architect drafts a new principle: Name: "Use Azure for Cloud Hosting." Statement: "All new workloads should support deployment on Microsoft Azure wherever possible." She submits it for Architecture Board approval, confident it's clear and actionable.

options.action: Approve the principle as written — it's clear, specific, and gives teams an unambiguous technology direction to follow.
options.rationale: Wrong on two counts the Standard specifically warns against: the Name mentions a specific technology platform (Azure), which the guidance explicitly says should not appear in the name or statement of a principle, and the Statement uses "support" and "wherever possible" — both flagged as ambiguous words to avoid.

options.action: Reject the principle for naming a specific vendor, but don't flag the ambiguous wording ("support," "wherever possible") as a separate problem.
options.rationale: Catches one real issue (naming Azure specifically) but misses the second, independent problem — the Statement's use of "support" and "wherever possible" is exactly the kind of ambiguous language the Standard's guidance warns against, regardless of the vendor-naming issue.

options.action: Reject the principle for two separate reasons: first, the Name and Statement both reference a specific technology platform (Azure), which the Standard's guidance explicitly says should not appear; second, the Statement uses ambiguous words ("support," "wherever possible") that the guidance specifically flags to avoid. Recommend a rewrite along the lines of: Name — "Cloud-First Hosting"; Statement — "New workloads are hosted on cloud infrastructure unless a documented constraint requires otherwise."
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly identifies both distinct problems named in the Standard's guidance (vendor-specificity and ambiguous wording) and offers a concrete rewrite that avoids both.

options.action: Approve the principle but add a footnote clarifying that "Azure" is just an example and other cloud providers are also acceptable.
options.rationale: Doesn't fix the actual problem — the issue isn't that only Azure was permitted, it's that naming any specific technology platform in a principle's Name or Statement violates the guidance at all; a footnote doesn't correct the structural flaw in how the principle itself is written.

lessonTitle: Architecture Principles — The Rules That Govern Everything
sourceRef: C220Part2e §3.8 — Enterprise Principles vs Architecture Principles hierarchy
scenario: A multinational's Enterprise Principles state: "All customer data must be processed transparently, with individuals able to access and correct their own records." The company's overseas IT division, seeking faster processing, proposes a subsidiary Architecture Principle stating: "For operational efficiency, customer record correction requests may be processed on a best-effort basis without a defined turnaround commitment."

options.action: Approve the subsidiary principle — Architecture Principles for a specific division are allowed to diverge from Enterprise Principles when local operational needs justify it.
options.rationale: Contradicts the hierarchy directly. Subsidiary (segment/divisional) principles must exist within the bounds of the overarching Enterprise Principles and cannot overstep their boundaries — a principle that weakens the enterprise-level commitment to transparent, correctable customer data access oversteps rather than elaborates on it.

options.action: Reject the subsidiary principle, but only on the grounds that it sounds vague, without connecting the rejection to the Enterprise/Architecture Principles hierarchy.
options.rationale: Reaches the right outcome but for an incomplete reason — the real issue is structural (a subsidiary principle cannot weaken or overstep the Enterprise Principle it sits beneath), not simply that the wording feels imprecise.

options.action: Reject the subsidiary principle: the hierarchy requires that subsidiary segment principles exist within the bounds of the overarching Enterprise Principles and cannot overstep their boundaries. Since the Enterprise Principle commits to individuals being able to access and correct their own records, a subsidiary principle that removes any defined turnaround commitment weakens that commitment rather than elaborating on it within bounds — it should be revised to specify a turnaround standard consistent with the Enterprise Principle, not to remove the commitment.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly applies the hierarchy rule (subsidiary principles must stay within Enterprise Principle bounds) and identifies exactly how the proposed principle oversteps rather than merely elaborates.

options.action: Suggest the overseas division simply ignore the new subsidiary principle informally, without any formal rejection or documented rationale.
options.rationale: Avoids the formal governance process entirely — a subsidiary principle proposal that conflicts with an Enterprise Principle should be formally rejected with documented rationale, not just informally ignored, since the informal approach leaves no record for future governance or audit.

lessonTitle: Architecture Principles — The Rules That Govern Everything
scenario: During a governance review, a stakeholder says: "Half of our Architecture Principles are just common sense — everyone already agrees with them, so why bother writing them down and enforcing them formally?"

options.action: Agree — principles that seem obvious to everyone can be safely dropped from formal documentation, since there's no real risk of anyone violating something so self-evident.
options.rationale: Misunderstands why principles are documented. A principle appearing self-evident doesn't mean it's consistently followed in practice — documenting even 'obvious' principles is precisely what ensures decisions actually follow the desired outcome, rather than assuming shared understanding guarantees shared behavior.

options.action: Disagree, but only argue that documentation is needed for audit purposes, without addressing why 'obvious' principles specifically still need enforcement.
options.rationale: Identifies a real benefit (audit trail) but misses the more direct point — that principles seeming obvious in the abstract doesn't prevent them from being violated in specific, pressured, real-world situations, which is exactly why formal documentation and enforcement still matters.

options.action: Disagree: a principle seeming self-evident on first reading doesn't mean the guidance it contains is reliably followed in practice, especially under real operational pressure. Formally documenting and governing even 'obvious' principles is what ensures decisions actually align with them — the appearance of consensus doesn't substitute for enforceable, referenceable guidance when a difficult trade-off arises.
options.rationale: Best answer — directly addresses the stakeholder's specific claim (obviousness implies safety to drop) and explains why formal documentation remains valuable precisely in the cases where a principle feels self-evident.

options.action: Suggest keeping only the principles nobody currently agrees with, since those are the ones that need enforcement, and dropping the ones with existing consensus.
options.rationale: Draws an unjustified and counterproductive distinction — principles with apparent consensus and no formal enforcement are just as capable of being quietly violated under pressure as contested ones; consensus at a point in time doesn't predict behavior in a specific difficult decision later.

lessonTitle: Architecture Principles — The Rules That Govern Everything
scenario: A CTO announces 47 new Architecture Principles at once, covering every conceivable technology decision the organization might ever face, and asks the architecture team to have all projects comply immediately.

options.action: Support the CTO's approach — more principles provide more complete guidance and reduce ambiguity for every possible situation.
options.rationale: Misunderstands the trade-off principles are meant to manage. An excessively large number of principles reduces architectural flexibility rather than improving guidance — the lesson's guidance on keeping principles few in number exists precisely because too many principles becomes unwieldy and self-defeating.

options.action: Push back on the number being too high, but recommend an arbitrary target of exactly 5 principles without further rationale.
options.rationale: Correctly identifies that 47 is excessive, but the specific alternative number isn't grounded in any stated reasoning — an unexplained arbitrary target doesn't help the CTO understand why a smaller, high-level set is preferable.

options.action: Push back on the scale: recommend consolidating toward a smaller set of high-level principles, since too many principles reduces architectural flexibility and becomes harder to apply consistently. Propose the team work with the CTO to identify which of the 47 are genuinely foundational versus which are more detailed standards or guidelines that could sit beneath a smaller set of core principles instead.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly identifies the core problem (too many principles undermines flexibility) and proposes a constructive path forward: distinguishing genuine foundational principles from more detailed standards that don't need to sit at the principle level at all.

options.action: Suggest all 47 be adopted immediately as written, but reviewed for possible consolidation in twelve months' time.
options.rationale: Defers a problem that should be addressed before roll-out — asking all projects to comply immediately with an unwieldy set of 47 principles risks a year of confused, inconsistent application before any consolidation happens, when the sizing issue could reasonably be addressed upfront instead.

lessonTitle: The Enterprise Continuum and Architecture Repository
sourceRef: C220-Part4e §6.6.1 — "should not be interpreted as representing strictly chained relationships"
scenario: An architect reviewing a new Organization-Specific Solution notices it directly incorporates a Foundation Solution component (a generic operating system), without passing through an intermediate Common Systems Solution or Industry Solution first. She flags this as a violation: "You can't skip levels in the Enterprise Continuum — Organization-Specific Solutions must be built from Industry Solutions, which come from Common Systems Solutions, which come from Foundation Solutions, in that strict order."

options.action: Agree — the four levels of the Continuum must be traversed strictly in sequence, and skipping directly from Foundation to Organization-Specific is not permitted.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard directly. It explicitly states the Enterprise Continuum should not be interpreted as representing strictly chained relationships — Organization-Specific Solutions could contain Foundation Solutions directly, without needing to pass through intermediate levels.

options.action: Disagree with the architect, but only say "the Continuum is more flexible than that" without citing the Standard's specific guidance on this point.
options.rationale: Reaches the correct conclusion but doesn't ground it — a stronger answer would cite the Standard's explicit statement about non-strict chaining, giving the architect a concrete basis to reconsider her review finding rather than a general reassurance.

options.action: Disagree, citing the Standard directly: it explicitly states the Enterprise Continuum should not be interpreted as representing strictly chained relationships, and gives the specific example that Organization-Specific Solutions could contain Foundation Solutions directly. Using a generic operating system (a Foundation Solution) directly within an Organization-Specific Solution is exactly the kind of leverage the Continuum is designed to enable, not a violation.
options.rationale: Best answer — directly rebuts the architect's claim using the Standard's own explicit language and named example, correcting a genuine misunderstanding of how the Continuum's levels relate to each other.

options.action: Suggest a compromise: allow skipping levels only for operating systems specifically, but require strict chaining for all other types of components.
options.rationale: Introduces an arbitrary, unsupported distinction — the Standard's guidance about non-strict chaining isn't limited to operating systems or any specific component type; it applies generally to how Continuum levels relate to each other.

lessonTitle: The Enterprise Continuum and Architecture Repository
sourceRef: C220Part0e §3.10, Figure 3-5 — Architecture Repository structure
scenario: An Architecture Board member asks where a newly approved Dispensation (a formal exception to an architecture standard) should be recorded within the Architecture Repository, and where the enterprise's list of approved integration patterns and templates should live.

options.action: Record both the Dispensation and the approved integration patterns/templates in the Standards Library, since both relate to compliance.
options.rationale: Wrong for both items. The Standards Library specifically captures standards new architectures must comply with — it isn't where governance decisions like Dispensations are recorded, and reusable patterns/templates belong in the Reference Library, not the Standards Library.

options.action: Correctly place the Dispensation in the Governance Repository, but also place the integration patterns/templates there too, on the grounds that both are 'governance-related.'
options.rationale: Gets the Dispensation placement right but misclassifies the patterns and templates — these are reusable reference material meant to accelerate the creation of new architectures, which is specifically the Reference Library's purpose, not the Governance Repository's.

options.action: Place the Dispensation in the Governance Repository, which provides a record of governance activity across the enterprise. Place the approved integration patterns and templates in the Reference Library, which provides guidelines, templates, patterns, and other reference material to accelerate the creation of new architectures.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly distinguishes the two components by their actual defined purposes: Governance Repository for governance activity records, Reference Library for reusable patterns and templates.

options.action: Suggest both items be stored in the Architecture Landscape, since that's the main repository component everyone thinks of first.
options.rationale: Misapplies the Architecture Landscape's actual purpose — it represents architectural assets deployed within the operating enterprise at a point in time, not governance decisions or reusable reference templates, which have their own dedicated repository components.

lessonTitle: The Enterprise Continuum and Architecture Repository
scenario: A new enterprise architect, unfamiliar with the distinction, tells her manager: "I've finished setting up our Architecture Repository — I don't think we also need to worry about the Enterprise Continuum separately, since they're really just two names for the same thing."

options.action: Agree — the Architecture Repository and Enterprise Continuum are interchangeable terms, so setting up one means the other is automatically covered.
options.rationale: Conflates two genuinely distinct concepts. The Architecture Repository is the actual storage structure holding architectural assets; the Enterprise Continuum is the classification scheme (generic to specific) used to understand and organize what's in that repository — one is the container, the other is the organizing lens.

options.action: Disagree, and say they're different, but describe the Enterprise Continuum simply as "a diagram" rather than explaining its actual classification function.
options.rationale: Correctly senses a distinction exists but doesn't accurately characterize what the Enterprise Continuum actually does — reducing it to "a diagram" undersells its function as a genuine classification and re-use mechanism for the assets stored in the Repository.

options.action: Disagree: the Architecture Repository is the structural framework that actually stores architectural assets (its Architecture Metamodel, Landscape, Standards Library, Reference Library, Governance Repository, and other components). The Enterprise Continuum is the classification scheme that organizes those same assets along a spectrum from generic (Foundation) to specific (Organization-Specific), helping architects find and re-use relevant assets. Setting up the Repository's structure doesn't automatically establish this classification discipline — that needs to be applied deliberately as assets are created and stored.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly explains both concepts and their genuine relationship (the Continuum organizes what the Repository stores), rather than treating them as either identical or entirely unrelated.

options.action: Suggest the Enterprise Continuum should be abandoned in favor of just using the Architecture Repository's structure alone, since having both seems redundant.
options.rationale: Misses that the two concepts serve complementary, non-redundant purposes — abandoning the classification scheme (Continuum) while keeping only the storage structure (Repository) would leave the enterprise with assets stored but with no discipline for understanding how generic or specific they are, undermining re-use.

lessonTitle: The Enterprise Continuum and Architecture Repository
scenario: A team lead says: "Before we design our own customer loyalty program architecture from scratch, let's check whether there's an existing Industry Architecture for retail loyalty programs we can start from — no point reinventing something the retail sector has probably already solved."

options.action: Agree with checking, but only look in the organization's own past projects rather than considering broader industry-level or common-systems-level reference architectures.
options.rationale: Takes a step in the right direction (checking before building from scratch) but searches too narrow a scope — restricting the search to the organization's own past projects misses the broader Enterprise Continuum principle of checking industry-wide and common-systems-level assets, not just internal history.

options.action: Strongly agree, and suggest searching the Enterprise Continuum systematically from the more generic end toward the specific: first check for a relevant Common Systems Architecture (e.g., a generic loyalty/rewards pattern), then an Industry Architecture (retail-specific loyalty program models), before considering building a fully Organization-Specific Architecture from scratch.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly applies the Enterprise Continuum's generic-to-specific search discipline, checking progressively more specific levels before committing to a fully custom build, which is the entire point of maintaining the Continuum.

options.action: Disagree — building from scratch is always preferable, since a custom-built architecture will better fit the organization's exact needs than any generic or industry reference model.
options.rationale: Contradicts the reuse principle that the Enterprise Continuum and Architecture Repository exist to support. Dismissing the value of checking for existing generic or industry patterns before building from scratch ignores the efficiency and quality benefits of leveraging proven, reusable assets.

options.action: Agree with the general idea, but suggest only checking for existing solutions rather than existing architectures, since solutions are what will actually be implemented.
options.rationale: Partially right in spirit but conflates the Architecture Continuum and Solutions Continuum — both are worth checking; architectural patterns (approaches, not necessarily deployable products) can meaningfully guide the design even before specific solution components are selected.

lessonTitle: The ADM — The Heart of TOGAF
sourceRef: C220-Part1e §13.5.1 — Requirements Management does not dispose of/prioritize requirements
scenario: During Phase C, three new requirements emerge simultaneously. The Requirements Management lead says: "As the owner of the Requirements Management process, I'll personally decide which of these three requirements takes priority, since that's exactly what Requirements Management is for."

options.action: Agree — since Requirements Management owns the process for handling requirements, prioritizing between competing new requirements is squarely within that role's authority.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard directly. It explicitly states the Requirements Management process itself does not dispose of, address, or prioritize any requirements — this is done within the relevant phase of the ADM, by the architects and stakeholders working in that phase, not by the Requirements Management function itself.

options.action: Disagree, and say prioritization should instead happen "somewhere else in the ADM," without identifying specifically where.
options.rationale: Correctly senses the lead has overstepped but doesn't identify the specific correct answer — the Standard specifically assigns this responsibility to the relevant phase currently active (in this case, Phase C), not to an unspecified other part of the ADM.

options.action: Disagree: Requirements Management is explicitly a process for managing and feeding requirements throughout the ADM — it does not itself dispose of, address, or prioritize them. Since these three requirements emerged during Phase C, prioritization should happen within Phase C, led by the architects responsible for that phase together with the relevant stakeholders, not unilaterally by the Requirements Management lead.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly cites the Standard's explicit limitation on Requirements Management's role and identifies exactly where prioritization authority actually sits: within the active ADM phase.

options.action: Suggest the three requirements be escalated directly to the Architecture Board for prioritization, bypassing Phase C entirely.
options.rationale: Skips a level unnecessarily — ordinary requirement prioritization during an active phase is the responsibility of that phase's architects and stakeholders; Architecture Board escalation is not the default routing for routine requirement prioritization within an ongoing phase.

lessonTitle: The ADM — The Heart of TOGAF
sourceRef: C220-Part1e §13.3, Step 10 — "gap requirement" definition
scenario: During gap analysis in Phase C, the team discovers that a data validation rule present in the Baseline Architecture does not appear anywhere in the Target Architecture. Investigation reveals this happened because the rule was simply overlooked when the Target was drafted — nobody made a deliberate decision to remove it. A team member says: "This is fine — anything missing from the Target compared to the Baseline is just an intentional simplification. Let's move on."

options.action: Agree — anything present in the Baseline but absent from the Target should be treated as an intentional simplification and requires no further action.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard's specific distinction. A gap requirement is defined as something eliminated by accident, requiring a change to the Target Architecture — this is different from a deliberate design decision to remove something. Treating an accidental omission as intentional risks losing a genuinely needed capability.

options.action: Disagree, and say the missing rule needs to be investigated, without using the specific term "gap requirement" or explaining the required next step of revising the Target Architecture.
options.rationale: Correctly senses a problem but doesn't apply the Standard's specific mechanism — identifying this as a gap requirement (something accidentally eliminated) and explaining that it must be addressed, documented, and the Target Architecture revised accordingly.

options.action: Disagree: since the investigation confirmed the omission was accidental rather than a deliberate decision, this is precisely what the Standard calls a gap requirement — something eliminated by accident that requires a change to the Target Architecture. It should be documented and recorded in the Architecture Requirements Repository, and the Target Architecture revised to restore the validation rule.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly applies the Standard's specific gap requirement definition to this exact scenario (accidental, not deliberate, omission) and identifies the required remediation: document and revise the Target Architecture.

options.action: Suggest simply adding the rule back into the Target Architecture directly, without any formal documentation or update to the Architecture Requirements Repository.
options.rationale: Fixes the immediate symptom but skips required process — the Standard specifies that gap requirements should be documented and recorded in the Architecture Requirements Repository as part of addressing them, not just silently patched into the Target Architecture.

lessonTitle: The ADM — The Heart of TOGAF
scenario: A programme sponsor asks: "Since the ADM diagram shows Phase A, then B, then C, then D in a circle, doesn't that mean we have to fully finish each phase before starting the next one, in strict order?"

options.action: Confirm the sponsor's understanding — the circular diagram represents a strict, sequential order that must be fully completed phase by phase.
options.rationale: Misreads the lesson's central point about the ADM. The graphic and discrete phase-by-phase description exist to communicate the basics clearly, but this presentation can be misread as implying a deterministic waterfall — which the ADM explicitly does not mandate.

options.action: Correct the sponsor by saying "it's more flexible than that," without explaining any of the specific ways the ADM can actually be applied iteratively.
options.rationale: Points in the right direction but doesn't give the sponsor anything concrete — a stronger answer would explain the actual mechanisms (phases running concurrently, cycling between phases, multiple parallel project cycles) that make this flexibility real rather than just asserted.

options.action: Correct the sponsor: the circular, sequential presentation is a communication convenience, not a mandate. In practice, phases can run concurrently (e.g., managing the interrelationship between Business, Information Systems, and Technology Architecture together), teams can cycle between phases in planned iterations to converge on a detailed Target Architecture, and separate projects can run their own ADM cycles concurrently with relationships between them.
options.rationale: Best answer — directly corrects the misconception and gives concrete, specific examples of how iteration actually works in practice, rather than a vague reassurance that flexibility exists.

options.action: Suggest that while phases don't need to be strictly sequential, at least all four core domain phases (B, C, D) must always run fully concurrently with each other on every project.
options.rationale: Replaces one rigid rule with another — the Standard doesn't mandate that Phases B, C, and D must always run fully concurrently either; concurrent phases are one legitimate iteration pattern among several, appropriate in some contexts and not others, not a new universal requirement.

lessonTitle: The ADM — The Heart of TOGAF
scenario: A junior team member asks: "If Requirements Management sits at the centre of the ADM and touches every phase, does that make it more important than the other phases — like the 'real' phase, with A through H just being supporting activities around it?"

options.action: Confirm this hierarchy — Requirements Management is the most important element, and Phases A through H exist to serve it.
options.rationale: Misrepresents the relationship. Requirements Management and the lettered phases serve different, complementary functions — Requirements Management manages the flow of requirements; the phases actually develop, govern, and evolve the architecture itself. Neither is subordinate to the other; they operate together.

options.action: Disagree, but simply say all parts of the ADM are 'equally important' without explaining what distinct role each actually plays.
options.rationale: Avoids the incorrect hierarchy but doesn't help the junior team member understand the actual relationship — a stronger answer explains what distinguishes Requirements Management's continuous role from the phases' developmental role.

options.action: Disagree with the hierarchy: Requirements Management and the lettered phases play different, complementary roles rather than one being subordinate to the other. Requirements Management is the continuous process that captures, stores, and feeds requirements to and from every phase — but it explicitly does not develop architecture content itself. Phases A through H are where the actual architecture work happens: developing Business, Data, Application, and Technology Architectures, planning migration, governing implementation, and managing change. Neither functions meaningfully without the other.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly frames the relationship as complementary rather than hierarchical, and explains the genuinely distinct function each part serves.

options.action: Suggest that Phase A is actually the most important phase since it's where the cycle begins, and Requirements Management is a minor supporting detail.
options.rationale: Introduces a different, equally unsupported hierarchy — Phase A being the starting point of a cycle doesn't make it more important than Requirements Management or the other phases; all parts of the ADM serve necessary, non-optional functions.

lessonTitle: Architecture Abstraction — The Four Levels
sourceRef: C220Part0e §3.7 — "why, what, and how have no connection to their use in the Zachman Framework"
scenario: An architect who previously worked with the Zachman Framework tells her new team: "TOGAF's abstraction levels use 'why,' 'what,' and 'how' — that's exactly the same structure as Zachman's framework, so anything I learned about applying those questions there transfers directly here."

options.action: Agree — since both frameworks use similar question words (why, what, how), her prior Zachman experience with these questions transfers directly to TOGAF's abstraction levels.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard directly. It explicitly notes that TOGAF's use of why, what, and how have no connection to their use in the Zachman Enterprise Architecture Framework — the surface similarity in wording does not imply the underlying concepts or usage transfer between the two frameworks.

options.action: Disagree, and say the two frameworks are "completely different" without acknowledging that some genuinely transferable architectural thinking skills might still carry over even though the specific abstraction-level framework doesn't.
options.rationale: Correctly identifies the frameworks are distinct in this respect but overstates the disconnect — general architectural thinking skills can still be valuable even though this specific why/what/how structure doesn't map between the two frameworks as she assumed.

options.action: Disagree specifically on this point: the Standard explicitly states that TOGAF's why/what/how/with-what abstraction levels have no connection to their use in the Zachman Framework, despite similar-sounding terminology. Her general architectural experience is valuable, but she should learn TOGAF's four abstraction levels (Contextual, Conceptual, Logical, Physical) as their own distinct concept rather than assuming a direct mapping from Zachman.
options.rationale: Best answer — precisely cites the Standard's explicit disclaimer and gives constructive guidance: general experience is useful, but this specific structural mapping doesn't hold and shouldn't be assumed.

options.action: Suggest she stop using Zachman terminology entirely and never reference her prior framework knowledge again while working with TOGAF.
options.rationale: Overcorrects unnecessarily — the issue is a specific, narrow point about the why/what/how question structure not mapping between frameworks; it doesn't follow that all prior architectural knowledge or vocabulary from Zachman must be discarded entirely.

lessonTitle: Architecture Abstraction — The Four Levels
sourceRef: C220Part0e §3.7.2 — Conceptual Abstraction Level, alternate names
scenario: In a design review, one architect refers to his work as being at the "Conceptual" level, while another architect on the same team describes what seems to be the exact same type of work as "service abstraction." A third team member suspects one of them has made an error.

options.action: Conclude one of them must be wrong, since "Conceptual" and "service abstraction" cannot refer to the same abstraction level.
options.rationale: Wrong. The Standard explicitly notes that the Conceptual Abstraction Level can also be referred to as either service abstraction or behavior abstraction — both architects may legitimately be describing the same level using accepted alternate terminology.

options.action: Suggest they're probably both fine, without citing that the Standard explicitly names "service abstraction" as an accepted alternate term for the Conceptual level.
options.rationale: Reaches a reasonable conclusion but doesn't ground it — confirming this with the Standard's specific alternate-naming guidance would give the team confidence rather than just an unsupported guess that it's probably fine.

options.action: Clarify that no error has necessarily occurred: the Standard explicitly states the Conceptual Abstraction Level can also be referred to as either service abstraction or behavior abstraction. Both architects are likely describing the same abstraction level using different accepted names for it, modeled using service models representing desired behavior.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly identifies that this is expected terminological variation explicitly sanctioned by the Standard, not a genuine disagreement or error.

options.action: Recommend the team stop using the term "service abstraction" going forward and standardize exclusively on "Conceptual" to avoid future confusion.
options.rationale: Unnecessary — since both terms are explicitly valid alternate names in the Standard, there's no requirement to eliminate one in favor of the other; the goal should be making sure the team understands both terms refer to the same level, not banning legitimate terminology.

lessonTitle: Architecture Abstraction — The Four Levels
scenario: A stakeholder reviewing an architecture package says: "I only see Conceptual and Logical level content here — nothing at the Contextual level. Does that matter, given we're a well-established department that's been operating the same way for a decade?"

options.action: Confirm it doesn't matter — well-established departments with a long operating history don't need Contextual-level content, since the environment and motivation are presumably already well understood by everyone involved.
options.rationale: Assumes familiarity substitutes for documentation. Contextual abstraction specifically captures the environment, goals, drivers, and objectives motivating the architecture work — even in a long-established department, this should be explicitly captured for this specific initiative, since "everyone already knows it" is an assumption, not a documented, shareable understanding.

options.action: Agree Contextual content should probably be added, but only for the sake of completeness, without explaining what specific value it adds beyond box-ticking.
options.rationale: Reaches a reasonable recommendation but doesn't articulate why Contextual content matters substantively — the real reason isn't process completeness for its own sake, but that Contextual content anchors the rest of the architecture in explicit goals, drivers, and scope, which prevents later disputes about intent.

options.action: Explain that Contextual content should still be included: it answers why the architecture work is needed, what its scope is, and what goals and drivers motivate it — this remains valuable even for an established department, since new stakeholders, new initiatives, or changing circumstances may not share the same implicit understanding that long-tenured staff have. Documenting it explicitly prevents assumptions from going unchallenged and gives future reviewers a clear anchor for evaluating whether the Conceptual and Logical content actually serves the stated goals.
options.rationale: Best answer — explains the substantive value of Contextual content (explicit goals/drivers/scope) rather than treating it as a formality, and connects it to why it matters even in a familiar, established context.

options.action: Suggest Contextual-level content should be added only if an external auditor specifically requests it, and otherwise can be skipped for internal-only architecture work.
options.rationale: Ties the decision to an arbitrary external trigger rather than the actual value the Contextual level provides — its usefulness for anchoring goals and scope doesn't depend on whether an auditor happens to ask for it.

lessonTitle: Architecture Abstraction — The Four Levels
scenario: An architect has documented, at the Logical level, that a "Notification Component" is needed with defined inputs, outputs, and interfaces — but implementation-independent. His manager asks him to also specify, at the same Logical-level document, exactly which cloud messaging product will be used and its specific configuration settings.

options.action: Comply immediately — adding the specific product and configuration details to the same Logical-level document makes it more complete and useful.
options.rationale: Conflates two distinct abstraction levels. The Logical level is specifically about identifying components in an implementation-independent fashion; adding a specific product and configuration details moves into Physical-level content, which should be a separate consideration, not folded into the same document.

options.action: Push back on adding the details to the same document, but without explaining which abstraction level the product and configuration details actually belong to.
options.rationale: Correctly resists conflating the two, but leaves the manager without a clear next step — identifying that this content belongs at the Physical level specifically would make the guidance actionable rather than just a refusal.

options.action: Explain that the Logical level is deliberately implementation-independent, and the specific product choice and configuration settings belong at the Physical level instead — which manages the allocation and implementation of physical components to meet the identified logical ones. Recommend producing a separate Physical-level document that references this Logical-level component and specifies how it will actually be realized.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly explains why the two levels should remain distinct and gives a constructive path forward (a separate Physical-level document) rather than either refusing outright or conflating the levels.

options.action: Suggest scrapping the Logical-level document entirely and starting over directly at the Physical level, skipping the Logical level altogether.
options.rationale: Discards valuable, correctly-produced work — the existing Logical-level document is not wrong; it simply shouldn't be merged with Physical-level content. Starting over unnecessarily wastes the implementation-independent analysis already completed.

lessonTitle: Architecture Views and Viewpoints
sourceRef: C220-Part4e §3.4.1 — Pilot/Air Traffic Controller example
