scenario: An architect produces a single combined view for both the warehouse operations team and the finance team on a new inventory system, arguing: "They're both looking at the same system, so one comprehensive view showing everything should serve both audiences perfectly well."

options.action: Agree — since both teams are stakeholders in the same system, a single comprehensive view covering all details is the most efficient way to serve both.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard's own illustrative reasoning. Using the pilot/air-traffic-controller example, the Standard shows that each stakeholder's viewpoint constrains and reduces how they see the overall system — the pilot cares about passengers and fuel, the controller cares about other planes; neither view completely describes the system, and combining them into one view for both audiences would serve neither well.

options.action: Disagree, and suggest producing two separate views, without explaining why combining them was actually problematic in the first place.
options.rationale: Reaches the right practical outcome but doesn't articulate the underlying principle — a stronger answer explains that each stakeholder group's concerns constrain what's relevant to them, similar to how the pilot and controller each need their own view despite observing the same airport system.

options.action: Disagree, and draw the parallel explicitly: like the pilot and air traffic controller in the Standard's own example — where each stakeholder's viewpoint constrains what's relevant to them (fuel and passengers for the pilot, other planes for the controller) even though they're observing the same airport system — the warehouse and finance teams should each receive a view built from a viewpoint addressing their specific concerns, rather than one undifferentiated view attempting to serve both.
options.rationale: Best answer — directly applies the Standard's own worked example to this new scenario, showing that shared subject matter doesn't mean shared viewing needs.

options.action: Suggest producing three views instead of two — one for warehouse, one for finance, and one combined view containing everything, in case anyone wants the full picture.
options.rationale: Unnecessarily reintroduces the same problem via the third view — a comprehensive combined view isn't inherently useful just because two audience-specific views also exist; if no stakeholder concern calls for the comprehensive view, it adds effort without any corresponding communication benefit.

lessonTitle: Architecture Views and Viewpoints
sourceRef: C220-Part4e §3.2.1 — fitness-for-purpose principle, "not reiterated ad infinitum as an academic exercise"
scenario: An architect has produced eleven detailed views for a mid-sized departmental system upgrade, addressing every stakeholder concern identified so far. A perfectionist colleague insists: "We should keep producing more views until we've achieved a truly complete and exhaustive description of the architecture from every conceivable angle — there's no such thing as too much documentation."

options.action: Agree — architecture work should continue producing views indefinitely to achieve the most exhaustive possible description, regardless of whether additional stakeholder concerns remain unaddressed.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard's explicit guidance directly. It states the architecture should be developed only to the point at which it is fit-for-purpose, and not reiterated ad infinitum as an academic exercise — producing views without a specific unaddressed stakeholder concern to justify them isn't the standard of completeness the Standard actually calls for.

options.action: Disagree, and say eleven views "seems like enough already," without connecting this back to the fitness-for-purpose principle or checking whether all pertinent stakeholder concerns have actually been addressed.
options.rationale: Reaches a reasonable practical instinct but doesn't apply the actual test the Standard specifies — the right question isn't a general sense of "enough," but whether all pertinent stakeholder concerns have been adequately addressed by the existing views.

options.action: Disagree, citing the Standard's principle of fitness-for-purpose: architecture should be developed only to the point at which it adequately addresses all pertinent stakeholder concerns, not reiterated indefinitely as an academic exercise. Since all identified stakeholder concerns are already addressed by the existing eleven views, recommend checking specifically for any remaining unaddressed concerns — and only producing additional views if a genuine gap is found, not for the sake of exhaustiveness itself.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly cites the Standard's specific fitness-for-purpose guidance and reframes the test as concern-coverage rather than volume, which is exactly the distinction the perfectionist colleague is missing.

options.action: Suggest capping the total number of views at exactly ten as a hard rule, regardless of whether all stakeholder concerns have actually been addressed.
options.rationale: Replaces one arbitrary standard (unlimited views) with another (a fixed cap) — the Standard's actual test is stakeholder concern coverage, not any particular number of views being the 'right' amount.

lessonTitle: Architecture Views and Viewpoints
scenario: A stakeholder asks an architect: "Can I get a viewpoint that just shows me the security aspects of this system?" The architect responds by immediately handing over a specific security diagram from a previous, unrelated project, saying: "Here's a viewpoint for you."

options.action: Confirm this is correct — handing over an existing diagram from another project satisfies the stakeholder's request for a viewpoint.
options.rationale: Confuses view and viewpoint. A specific diagram from a previous project is a view (a representation specific to the architecture it was created for) — the stakeholder's request for a "viewpoint" (if meant precisely) would call for the underlying specification/template, or more likely, given the context, the stakeholder actually wants a new view built for this system, not a reused artifact from an unrelated one.

options.action: Point out the general confusion between view and viewpoint, without clarifying what the architect should actually do to properly address the stakeholder's request.
options.rationale: Identifies that something is conceptually off but doesn't resolve the practical question — what the architect should have done: use an existing security viewpoint (if one exists in the viewpoint library) as a template to produce a new view specific to the current system, rather than handing over an unrelated project's finished view.

options.action: Clarify the distinction: what the architect handed over is a view — a representation specific to the previous project's architecture, not this one. If a security viewpoint already exists in the organization's viewpoint library, the architect should use it as a template to generate a new view specific to the current system's security aspects, since a view is always specific to the architecture for which it is created and can't simply be reused as-is from an unrelated system.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly distinguishes the reusable viewpoint (template) from the specific view (instance), and identifies the correct action: use the viewpoint as a template to build a new, appropriate view for this stakeholder's actual system.

options.action: Suggest the stakeholder should have asked for a "model" instead of a "viewpoint," since that's the more precise term for what they actually want.
options.rationale: Introduces an unhelpful terminology correction rather than addressing the substantive problem — the core issue is that a view from an unrelated project was handed over as though it were reusable, not that the stakeholder used slightly imprecise vocabulary in their original request.

lessonTitle: Architecture Views and Viewpoints
scenario: During a governance review, an auditor asks to see the architecture viewpoint used to produce a particular network diagram in the Architecture Definition Document. The architect says: "There's no viewpoint for this — I just drew the diagram directly based on what seemed useful at the time."

options.action: Accept this explanation at face value — since no formal viewpoint document exists, this particular view genuinely has no associated viewpoint.
options.rationale: Misunderstands a key point about views and viewpoints. Every architecture view has an associated architecture viewpoint that describes it, at least implicitly — even if the architect didn't consciously write one down, the conventions, stakeholder concerns, and modeling choices that shaped the diagram constitute an implicit viewpoint that could be made explicit.

options.action: Push back and ask the architect to write a viewpoint "after the fact," without explaining that this is a legitimate, recognized practice rather than an unusual workaround.
options.rationale: Reaches a reasonable practical suggestion but doesn't reassure the architect this is a normal, expected approach — retroactively making an implicit viewpoint explicit (so it can be saved and reused) is a recognized way of building a viewpoint library, not an irregular fix.

options.action: Explain that every architecture view has an associated viewpoint, at least implicitly — even without formal documentation, the choices the architect made (which stakeholders and concerns the diagram addresses, what modeling conventions were used) constitute an implicit viewpoint. Suggest making this viewpoint explicit now and saving it to the organization's viewpoint library, so this style of network diagram can be efficiently reused as a template for future, similar architecture engagements.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly explains that an implicit viewpoint necessarily exists, and turns the governance finding into a constructive outcome: formalizing and reusing the pattern going forward.

options.action: Recommend the diagram be discarded entirely from the Architecture Definition Document, since it lacks a formally documented viewpoint.
options.rationale: Disproportionate — the absence of a formally written-down viewpoint doesn't mean the view itself is invalid or unusable; it simply means the implicit viewpoint hasn't yet been made explicit, which is a documentation gap to close, not a reason to discard otherwise valid architectural content.

lessonTitle: The Preliminary Phase
sourceRef: C220-Part1e §2.5 — "Preliminary Phase may be revisited, from the Architecture Vision phase"
scenario: During Phase A stakeholder analysis, the architecture team discovers that the organization's existing Architecture Capability — established during the Preliminary Phase two years ago — has no defined process for governing cloud security architecture, which is now central to the current engagement's scope. A team member says: "We're already in Phase A, so we just have to work around this gap as best we can within the current phase."

options.action: Agree — once the ADM has progressed to Phase A, the Preliminary Phase is finished and cannot be revisited; the team must work around any capability gaps within Phase A itself.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard directly. It explicitly states the Preliminary Phase may be revisited from the Architecture Vision phase, specifically to ensure the organization's Architecture Capability is suitable to address a specific architecture problem — which is exactly the situation described here.

options.action: Disagree, and suggest going back to address the gap, without specifically identifying this as a legitimate, named return to the Preliminary Phase.
options.rationale: Reaches a reasonable practical instinct but doesn't recognize the formal mechanism — the Standard specifically anticipates and names this situation as revisiting the Preliminary Phase, which gives the team clear governance language to use rather than an ad hoc workaround.

options.action: Disagree: the Standard explicitly anticipates this exact situation — the Preliminary Phase may be revisited from the Architecture Vision phase specifically to ensure the organization's Architecture Capability is suitable to address a specific architecture problem. Recommend formally returning to extend the Architecture Capability with cloud security governance processes before continuing Phase A, rather than working around the gap informally.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly identifies the Standard's specific, named provision for this exact situation and recommends the proper formal action rather than an ad hoc workaround.

options.action: Suggest the entire ADM cycle must restart from a fresh Preliminary Phase before any further Phase A work can continue.
options.rationale: Overcorrects — revisiting the Preliminary Phase to extend the Architecture Capability for a specific gap doesn't require discarding all Phase A progress and restarting the entire cycle from scratch; it's a targeted extension, not a full reset.

lessonTitle: The Preliminary Phase
sourceRef: C220-Part1e §2.1 — Two objectives (Determine vs Establish the Architecture Capability)
scenario: A new Chief Architect summarizes the Preliminary Phase to his team as having one single objective: "To establish the Architecture Capability the organization needs." A colleague reviewing his summary slide says something seems incomplete.

options.action: Confirm the summary is complete — establishing the Architecture Capability is the sole objective of the Preliminary Phase.
options.rationale: Wrong. The Standard defines two distinct objectives for the Preliminary Phase: first, to determine the Architecture Capability desired by the organization (reviewing context, scoping, identifying frameworks, setting a maturity target); second, to establish that capability. The summary captures only the second objective, missing the first entirely.

options.action: Point out that something is missing, without specifying what the first objective (determining the desired capability) actually involves.
options.rationale: Correctly identifies an incompleteness but doesn't name the missing objective or its content — a stronger answer would specify that 'determining' the desired capability (reviewing context, scoping affected organizations, identifying intersecting frameworks, setting maturity targets) precedes and is distinct from 'establishing' it.

options.action: Point out the summary is missing an entire objective: the Preliminary Phase has two objectives, not one — first, determining the Architecture Capability desired (reviewing organizational context, scoping affected elements, identifying intersecting frameworks, and establishing a maturity target), and second, establishing that capability (defining the Organizational Model, governance processes, tools, and Architecture Principles). The slide captures only the second objective.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly identifies both distinct objectives by name and explains what each one specifically involves, showing precisely what the summary omitted.

options.action: Suggest the summary should instead say the Preliminary Phase has three objectives, adding "maintaining the Architecture Capability" as a third.
options.rationale: Introduces an objective not defined in the Standard for this phase — the Preliminary Phase's two stated objectives are determining and establishing the capability; ongoing maintenance and evolution of the capability is addressed elsewhere in the ADM (e.g., Phase H), not as a third Preliminary Phase objective.

lessonTitle: The Preliminary Phase
scenario: A CFO asks: "Why does the Preliminary Phase need its own dedicated budget line? Surely the cost of setting up 'how we do architecture' should just be absorbed into the first project that needs an architecture."

options.action: Agree — Preliminary Phase costs are minor enough to fold into the first project's budget without any separate justification.
options.rationale: Understates the nature of Preliminary Phase work. Establishing the Architecture Capability — governance processes, tooling, principles, organizational model — is enterprise-wide infrastructure meant to serve every future architecture engagement, not a cost specific to whichever project happens to go first; folding it into one project's budget risks that project unfairly bearing costs that benefit the whole organization.

options.action: Disagree, but justify it only by saying "architecture needs a budget too," without explaining why the cost is enterprise-wide rather than project-specific.
options.rationale: Reaches a reasonable conclusion but doesn't make the underlying case — the CFO needs to understand that Preliminary Phase costs fund reusable capability for all future engagements, not simply that architecture work in general costs money.

options.action: Disagree, and explain that the Preliminary Phase establishes capability — governance processes, tooling, Architecture Principles, and an organizational model — intended to serve every future architecture engagement, not just the first project. Funding it as enterprise-wide infrastructure, rather than folding it into one project's budget, ensures the cost is fairly attributed to its actual, ongoing beneficiaries rather than unfairly burdening whichever project happens to be first.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly explains why Preliminary Phase costs are properly treated as enterprise infrastructure investment, distinct from and not fairly absorbed by any single project's budget.

options.action: Suggest splitting the Preliminary Phase cost evenly across exactly the first three projects that use the resulting Architecture Capability, regardless of relative usage.
options.rationale: Introduces an arbitrary allocation method not grounded in the actual point — the specific number of projects and even split isn't the real issue; the point is that Preliminary Phase costs support the capability broadly and shouldn't be treated as any specific project's cost at all, whether split three ways or absorbed by one.

lessonTitle: The Preliminary Phase
scenario: An organization with three semi-autonomous regional divisions is beginning its first TOGAF adoption. Each division currently uses different informal architecture practices. The corporate CIO asks: "Should we mandate one single organization-wide architecture team structure during the Preliminary Phase, or can each division keep something different?"

options.action: Mandate one single, identical team structure for all three divisions, since consistency is always the priority and no division-specific variation should be permitted.
options.rationale: Overstates the requirement for uniformity. The Preliminary Phase's steps should be adapted to the situation at hand, and organizations may need to consider partitioning approaches for architecture teams, processes, and deliverables depending on scale and structure — semi-autonomous divisions may legitimately warrant some structural variation rather than one forced-identical model.

options.action: Suggest each division should keep its current informal practice entirely unchanged, with no coordination or common framework established at all.
options.rationale: Goes too far the other way — while some divisional variation may be appropriate, the Preliminary Phase exists precisely to establish a coherent Architecture Capability; leaving three entirely disconnected informal practices in place misses the point of adopting a common framework and governance approach in the first place.

options.action: Recommend the Preliminary Phase explicitly address architecture partitioning for this specific situation: establish a common overall framework, governance approach, and set of Architecture Principles at the enterprise level, while considering whether some divisional-level variation in team structure or process detail is warranted given their semi-autonomous status — adapting the level of formality and touch-points between divisions and the centre as part of the Preliminary Phase's own approach.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly recognizes that the Preliminary Phase should establish enterprise-level coherence while adapting to organizational context, rather than forcing either total uniformity or total divisional independence.

options.action: Suggest deferring any decision about team structure until after the first full ADM cycle is complete, treating it as an unrelated concern from the Preliminary Phase.
options.rationale: Misplaces this decision — team structure and organizational model are specifically Preliminary Phase outputs (the Organizational Model for Enterprise Architecture); deferring this decision until after a full ADM cycle leaves the first cycle without a clear architecture team structure to operate under.

lessonTitle: Phase A — Architecture Vision
sourceRef: C220-Part1e §3.4 — "Multiple business scenarios may be used to generate a single Architecture Vision"
scenario: During Phase A, the team has developed three separate Business Scenarios addressing different stakeholder concerns: one for the finance team's reporting needs, one for operations' process efficiency concerns, and one for the compliance team's audit requirements. A team member says: "We can only use one Business Scenario per Architecture Vision — we'll need to pick the most important one and set the other two aside."

options.action: Agree — only one Business Scenario can inform a single Architecture Vision, so the team must select the most important one and discard the others.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard directly. It explicitly notes that multiple business scenarios may be used to generate a single Architecture Vision — there's no requirement to select only one; discarding two legitimately developed scenarios addressing real stakeholder concerns is unnecessary and wasteful.

options.action: Disagree, and say all three scenarios can somehow be used together, without citing that the Standard explicitly permits this or explaining how they'd be integrated.
options.rationale: Reaches the correct conclusion but doesn't ground it in the Standard's specific guidance — citing the explicit statement that multiple scenarios may generate a single vision gives the team clear authority to proceed, rather than an unsupported assertion.

options.action: Disagree: the Standard explicitly states multiple business scenarios may be used to generate a single Architecture Vision. All three scenarios — addressing finance reporting, operations efficiency, and compliance audit concerns — can and should inform the same Architecture Vision, since they represent genuine, distinct stakeholder concerns that the Vision should reflect collectively.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly cites the Standard's explicit permission for multiple scenarios feeding one Vision, and explains why using all three serves the actual purpose of capturing diverse stakeholder concerns.

options.action: Suggest producing three separate Architecture Visions, one for each Business Scenario, rather than one combined Vision.
options.rationale: Overcorrects into unnecessary duplication — the Standard specifically supports multiple scenarios feeding into a single Vision; producing three separate Visions fragments what should be one coherent, aspirational picture of the Target Architecture for this engagement.

lessonTitle: Phase A — Architecture Vision
sourceRef: C220-Part1e §3.5.2 — consensus represented by sponsoring organization signing the Statement of Architecture Work
scenario: An architecture team has completed a polished, detailed Architecture Vision document and circulated it widely by email for informal feedback. The CTO reads it and replies: "Looks great, thanks!" The team lead declares: "We have consensus — the CTO's email approval means we can proceed to Phase B."

options.action: Agree — an informal positive email reply from the CTO constitutes the consensus needed to proceed to Phase B.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard's specific guidance. It states that consensus is represented by the sponsoring organization formally signing the Statement of Architecture Work — an informal, casual email reply to the Architecture Vision document is not equivalent to this formal governance step.

options.action: Disagree, and say more formal approval is needed, without specifying exactly what document requires signing or by whom.
options.rationale: Correctly senses the informal email isn't sufficient but doesn't identify the precise requirement — the Standard specifically names the Statement of Architecture Work as the document requiring the sponsoring organization's formal sign-off.

options.action: Disagree: the Standard specifies that consensus is represented by the sponsoring organization formally signing the Statement of Architecture Work, not by an informal email reply to the Architecture Vision document. Recommend finalizing and formally submitting the Statement of Architecture Work for the sponsoring organization's signature before treating Phase A as complete and proceeding to Phase B.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly identifies the specific formal governance step the Standard requires (signed Statement of Architecture Work) and distinguishes it from the informal email approval that occurred instead.

options.action: Suggest the team proceed to Phase B immediately, and retroactively obtain a signed Statement of Architecture Work sometime before Phase B concludes.
options.rationale: Reverses the required sequence — the Standard's guidance is that consensus (via the signed Statement of Architecture Work) is what enables proceeding to subsequent phases, not something to be arranged retroactively after work has already moved forward.

lessonTitle: Phase A — Architecture Vision
scenario: A Phase A team has identified stakeholders and drafted an Architecture Vision, but has not yet assessed whether the organization is actually ready to absorb the scale of change being proposed. The programme sponsor says: "We know what we want to build — let's move straight to the Statement of Architecture Work and secure approval."

options.action: Agree — once stakeholders are identified and a vision is drafted, moving directly to securing approval is the natural next step, regardless of organizational readiness.
options.rationale: Skips a distinct, necessary Phase A step. Assessing readiness for business transformation is a defined activity within Phase A, separate from stakeholder identification and vision drafting — proceeding to secure approval without this assessment risks approving a Statement of Architecture Work for change the organization isn't actually prepared to absorb.

options.action: Push back and suggest a readiness assessment should happen, but describe it as optional or 'nice to have' rather than a defined step in Phase A.
options.rationale: Correctly identifies the gap but understates its status — assessing readiness for business transformation is one of the specifically defined steps within Phase A, not an optional add-on to consider only if time permits.

options.action: Push back: assessing readiness for business transformation is a specifically defined Phase A step, distinct from identifying stakeholders and drafting the vision. Recommend completing this readiness assessment before finalizing the Statement of Architecture Work, since proceeding to secure approval without it risks committing the organization to a scope of change it may not be prepared to absorb.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly identifies readiness assessment as a specific, required Phase A step and explains the concrete risk of skipping it before securing formal approval.

options.action: Suggest the readiness assessment be conducted after the Statement of Architecture Work is signed, as a Phase B activity instead.
options.rationale: Misplaces the activity to the wrong phase — assessing readiness for business transformation is a Phase A step feeding into the Architecture Vision and Statement of Architecture Work, not something deferred to Phase B after approval has already been secured.

lessonTitle: Phase A — Architecture Vision
scenario: A Phase A team produces an Architecture Vision that includes ambitious value propositions and KPIs, but the accompanying Statement of Architecture Work contains no mention of how or when these will be tracked. A stakeholder asks how the organization will know if the vision's promised benefits actually materialize.

options.action: Respond that KPIs and value propositions are aspirational statements in the Architecture Vision only, and don't need to be formally incorporated anywhere else.
options.rationale: Misses a specific linkage the Standard establishes. Performance metrics and measures defined when developing Target Architecture value propositions and KPIs should be incorporated within the Statement of Architecture Work specifically so that performance can be tracked accordingly — leaving them only in the aspirational Vision document, disconnected from the tracking mechanism, undermines their purpose.

options.action: Agree the KPIs should be tracked somewhere, but suggest an entirely new, separate tracking document rather than incorporating them into the existing Statement of Architecture Work.
options.rationale: Solves the immediate concern but creates unnecessary duplication — the Standard specifically directs that these outputs be incorporated within the Statement of Architecture Work itself, which already exists as the natural home for this information, rather than creating a new parallel document.

options.action: Explain that the value propositions and KPIs, along with performance metrics and measures, should be incorporated within the Statement of Architecture Work specifically so that performance can be tracked accordingly. Recommend updating the Statement of Architecture Work to include this tracking mechanism before finalizing Phase A, rather than leaving the KPIs as an aspirational statement disconnected from any accountability structure.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly identifies where the Standard specifies this information should live (the Statement of Architecture Work) and explains why that placement matters for actual accountability.

options.action: Suggest the KPIs don't need formal tracking at all until Phase G Implementation Governance begins.
options.rationale: Defers something that should already be established during Phase A — the Standard's guidance is that KPIs and performance metrics are incorporated into the Statement of Architecture Work as part of Phase A itself, precisely so that tracking can begin from the point of approval, not deferred until much later in the ADM cycle.

lessonTitle: Phase B — Business Architecture
sourceRef: C220-Part1e §4.1 — Phase B two objectives (Target Business Architecture + candidate Roadmap components)
scenario: A Phase B team produces a comprehensive Target Business Architecture describing exactly how the enterprise needs to operate to achieve its business goals. The team lead declares Phase B complete and ready to move to Phase C. A colleague asks whether anything else was supposed to come out of this phase.

options.action: Confirm Phase B is complete — developing the Target Business Architecture is the sole objective of the phase.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard directly. Phase B has two explicit objectives: developing the Target Business Architecture, and identifying candidate Architecture Roadmap components based on gaps between the Baseline and Target Business Architectures. Only the first has been completed.

options.action: Point out something is missing, without specifically naming the second objective (candidate Architecture Roadmap components from gap analysis).
options.rationale: Correctly senses incompleteness but doesn't identify what's actually missing — a stronger answer names the specific second objective and explains it requires comparing Baseline to Target to identify gaps.

options.action: Point out that Phase B has two objectives, not one: alongside developing the Target Business Architecture, the team must also identify candidate Architecture Roadmap components based on gaps between the Baseline and Target Business Architectures. This requires a Baseline Business Architecture and a formal gap analysis, neither of which has been mentioned — Phase B is not yet complete.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly names both Phase B objectives and identifies exactly what's missing (Baseline Architecture and gap analysis) before the phase can be considered complete.

options.action: Suggest the missing work can simply be completed later during Phase E instead, without revisiting Phase B.
options.rationale: Misplaces the responsibility — identifying candidate Architecture Roadmap components based on Business Architecture gaps is specifically a Phase B objective; Phase E consolidates gap analysis results from Phases B, C, and D, but doesn't perform Phase B's own gap analysis on its behalf.

lessonTitle: Phase B — Business Architecture
sourceRef: C220-Part1e §4.2.3 — Phase B inputs include Capability Assessment and Communications Plan from Phase A
scenario: A Phase B team begins their work without referencing anything produced during Phase A, arguing: "Phase B is about business architecture, and Phase A was about vision and stakeholders — they're separate concerns, so we don't need anything from Phase A as an input."

options.action: Agree — Phase B can proceed entirely independently of Phase A's outputs, since the two phases address distinct concerns.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard directly. Phase B's defined inputs explicitly include several Phase A outputs: the Capability Assessment, the Communications Plan, the approved Statement of Architecture Work, and the Architecture Vision itself — these are not optional references but named required inputs.

options.action: Disagree, and say Phase B needs 'some' input from Phase A, without specifying which particular outputs are required.
options.rationale: Correctly senses a dependency exists but doesn't name what's actually required — a stronger answer specifically identifies the Capability Assessment, Communications Plan, Statement of Architecture Work, and Architecture Vision as named Phase B inputs.

options.action: Disagree: Phase B's defined inputs specifically include several Phase A outputs — the Capability Assessment, Communications Plan, approved Statement of Architecture Work, and the Architecture Vision itself, including its problem description and refined stakeholder requirements. Phase B should draw directly on these rather than starting as though Phase A never happened.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly names the specific Phase A outputs that serve as required Phase B inputs, showing precisely how the two phases connect rather than asserting a vague general dependency.

options.action: Suggest Phase B only needs the Architecture Vision from Phase A, and can safely disregard the Capability Assessment, Communications Plan, and Statement of Architecture Work.
options.rationale: Only partially corrects the error — while the Architecture Vision is indeed a required input, the Capability Assessment, Communications Plan, and Statement of Architecture Work are also explicitly listed as Phase B inputs and shouldn't be disregarded either.

lessonTitle: Phase B — Business Architecture
scenario: A Phase B team, under time pressure, decides to skip developing a Baseline Business Architecture entirely: "We already know roughly what the current processes look like from experience — let's just focus our effort on the Target Business Architecture and save time."

options.action: Support skipping the Baseline entirely — informal team experience with current processes is a sufficient substitute for a documented Baseline Business Architecture.
options.rationale: Undermines the gap analysis Phase B is specifically meant to produce. Without a properly developed Baseline, there's no rigorous basis for identifying gaps between current and target states — informal recollection risks missing undocumented processes, dependencies, or constraints that a systematic Baseline development would surface.

options.action: Push back on skipping the Baseline, but only for general thoroughness reasons, without connecting this to the specific gap analysis objective it supports.
options.rationale: Reaches a reasonable conclusion but misses the specific mechanism — the real reason a Baseline matters is that Phase B's second objective (identifying candidate Roadmap components) depends on a genuine gap analysis between Baseline and Target, which informal recollection can't rigorously support.

options.action: Push back: skipping the Baseline undermines Phase B's second objective — identifying candidate Architecture Roadmap components based on gaps between Baseline and Target Business Architectures. Informal team experience isn't a substitute for a properly developed Baseline; without it, gap analysis becomes guesswork, risking missed dependencies or undocumented processes that only surface through systematic Baseline development.
options.rationale: Best answer — directly connects the risk of skipping the Baseline to the specific Phase B objective it undermines, explaining precisely why rigor here matters rather than asserting a general principle.

options.action: Suggest developing a full, exhaustive Baseline covering every conceivable business process in complete detail, regardless of relevance to this engagement's scope.
options.rationale: Overcorrects into excessive scope — the level of Baseline detail should depend on the scope and goals of the overall architecture effort; an exhaustive, maximally detailed Baseline covering irrelevant processes wastes effort without improving the quality of the specific gap analysis this engagement needs.

lessonTitle: Phase B — Business Architecture
scenario: A Phase B architect has produced a comprehensive Target Business Architecture but hasn't yet checked the Architecture Repository for any existing, reusable business capability models or reference architectures relevant to the organization's industry. A colleague suggests this check should happen before finalizing the work.

options.action: Dismiss the suggestion — since the architecture was custom-built specifically for this organization, checking the Repository for existing reusable assets is an unnecessary extra step.
options.rationale: Ignores the value of the Architecture Repository and Enterprise Continuum's reuse principle. Phase B specifically calls for considering relevant Business Architecture resources from the Architecture Repository, including industry reference models and enterprise-specific building blocks — skipping this check risks reinventing work that already exists in a usable form.

options.action: Agree the check should happen, but treat it as a nice-to-have quality improvement rather than a defined part of the Phase B approach.
options.rationale: Reaches the right practical conclusion but understates its status — considering relevant Architecture Repository resources (industry reference models, enterprise-specific views and building blocks) is specifically part of Phase B's defined approach, not an optional polish step.

options.action: Agree the check should happen: Phase B's approach specifically calls for considering relevant Business Architecture resources available in the Architecture Repository — including industry reference models relevant to the organization's sector, enterprise-specific views like capability and value stream maps, and reusable building blocks. This check should occur before finalizing the Target Business Architecture, not as an afterthought.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly identifies this as a defined part of the Phase B approach itself, not an optional extra, and specifies the types of reusable assets that should be checked.

options.action: Suggest the Repository check only matters if the organization operates in a heavily regulated industry with mandatory reference models.
options.rationale: Introduces an unsupported restriction — the Standard's guidance to consider Architecture Repository resources during Phase B isn't limited to regulated industries; the value of checking for reusable capability maps, value stream maps, and building blocks applies generally, regardless of regulatory context.

lessonTitle: Phase C — Information Systems Architectures
sourceRef: C220-Part1e §7.3.1.3 — "it may be appropriate to drop into a short iteration of the Data Architecture"
scenario: While mapping applications to business services during Application Architecture work, a team discovers that baseline application data models reveal significant undocumented data quality issues affecting several core applications. A team member says: "We're doing Application Architecture right now — data issues are out of scope until we formally reach the Data Architecture sub-phase, whenever that's scheduled."

options.action: Agree — data issues discovered during Application Architecture work must wait until the Data Architecture sub-phase is formally scheduled to begin, regardless of what's found.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard's own guidance. It explicitly notes that at this point in Application Architecture work, it may be appropriate to drop into a short iteration of the Data Architecture if deemed valuable to the scope of the engagement — rigid phase boundaries aren't meant to block addressing significant issues discovered mid-stream.

options.action: Disagree, and suggest looking into the data issues now, without citing that the Standard specifically anticipates and supports this kind of short, valuable iteration.
options.rationale: Reaches a reasonable practical instinct but doesn't ground it — citing the Standard's specific allowance for dropping into a short Data Architecture iteration gives the team clear authority to proceed rather than an informal workaround.

options.action: Disagree: the Standard explicitly states that at this point in Application Architecture work, it may be appropriate to drop into a short iteration of Data Architecture if deemed valuable to the scope of the engagement. Since significant undocumented data quality issues have been found affecting core applications, a short, focused Data Architecture iteration now — rather than waiting for a rigidly scheduled sub-phase — is exactly the kind of situation this guidance anticipates.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly cites the Standard's specific, named allowance for this exact situation and applies it directly to the discovered data quality issues.

options.action: Suggest pausing all Phase C work entirely and returning fully to Phase B until the data issues are resolved.
options.rationale: Overcorrects — the Standard's guidance is for a short, targeted iteration into Data Architecture specifically, not a full return to an earlier phase (Business Architecture) that has no direct bearing on the data quality issues discovered.

lessonTitle: Phase C — Information Systems Architectures
sourceRef: C220-Part1e §6.5.2.3 — Data Governance three dimensions (Structure, Management System, People)
scenario: An organization undertaking a large-scale data transformation focuses its data governance planning entirely on writing new data management policies and procedures, believing this single dimension covers everything data governance requires.

options.action: Confirm this is a complete data governance approach — policies and procedures are the entirety of what data governance requires.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard directly. It identifies three distinct dimensions of data governance: Structure (organizational structure and standards bodies), Management System (systems and programs managing data throughout its lifecycle), and People (the skills and roles required) — policies and procedures alone address only part of the Management System dimension, leaving Structure and People unaddressed.

options.action: Point out something is missing from the approach, without naming the specific dimensions (Structure, Management System, People) that the Standard identifies.
options.rationale: Correctly senses incompleteness but doesn't specify what's actually missing — a stronger answer names all three dimensions and explains that policies alone don't address organizational structure or the people/skills dimension.

options.action: Point out that data governance requires three distinct dimensions, not just policies: Structure (whether the necessary organizational structure and standards bodies exist), Management System (systems and data-related programs to manage governance throughout the data lifecycle), and People (the data-related skills and roles the enterprise requires, acquired or developed through training if lacking). Writing policies alone addresses only part of the Management System dimension.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly names all three data governance dimensions from the Standard and explains specifically what the current approach is missing.

options.action: Suggest the organization only needs to add a People dimension (training plans) to complete its data governance approach, since Structure isn't typically a real concern.
options.rationale: Only partially corrects the gap — Structure (organizational structure and standards bodies) is one of three named dimensions in the Standard, not something to dismiss as not typically a concern; all three dimensions require attention, not just People.

lessonTitle: Phase C — Information Systems Architectures
scenario: A team building the Application Portfolio Catalog for a new engagement wants to begin by producing detailed Application Communication diagrams first, arguing: "Diagrams communicate better with stakeholders, so let's start there and build the catalog afterward from what the diagrams show."

options.action: Support starting with diagrams — since they communicate more effectively with stakeholders, building them before the catalog is a reasonable sequencing choice.
options.rationale: Inverts the typical, sensible construction order. The Application Portfolio Catalog is typically the starting point of the Application Architecture phase, providing the foundation on which matrices and diagrams are built — starting with diagrams before an agreed catalog exists risks the diagrams lacking a stable, agreed inventory to draw from.

options.action: Push back on starting with diagrams, but without explaining why the catalog specifically serves as the necessary foundation for what follows.
options.rationale: Reaches a reasonable objection but doesn't explain the underlying logic — the catalog isn't just 'more proper' to do first arbitrarily; it specifically provides the foundational list of applications that matrices and diagrams are then built from.

options.action: Push back: the Application Portfolio Catalog is typically the starting point of the Application Architecture phase, providing the foundation on which the remaining matrices and diagrams are based. Recommend establishing the catalog first — even if diagrams will ultimately be more effective for stakeholder communication — since diagrams built before an agreed, complete application inventory exists risk being based on an incomplete or inconsistent picture.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly identifies the catalog's role as the structural foundation and explains the specific risk of reversing this order, while acknowledging the team's underlying (valid) point about diagrams' communication value.

options.action: Suggest producing the catalog and diagrams simultaneously in a fully parallel, uncoordinated fashion with no dependency between them.
options.rationale: Misses the actual relationship between the two artifacts — diagrams are meant to be built from and remain consistent with the catalog; producing them with no coordination risks the two artifacts showing conflicting or incompatible information about the same application landscape.

lessonTitle: Phase C — Information Systems Architectures
scenario: A Data Architect produces a Data Entity/Business Function Matrix showing which business functions create, read, update, and delete each data entity. The Application Architecture team, working separately, produces an Application/Data Matrix covering similar ground. A stakeholder asks whether one of these two matrices is redundant and should be dropped.

options.action: Recommend dropping one of the two matrices, since both seem to cover the relationship between organizational elements and data.
options.rationale: Conflates two distinct matrices serving different governance purposes. The Data Entity/Business Function Matrix supports assigning data ownership and enabling data governance programs at the business-function level; the Application/Data Matrix supports understanding which applications technically create, read, update, and delete data — these serve different analytical and governance needs, not a redundant overlap.

options.action: Recommend keeping both matrices, but without explaining the distinct purpose each one serves.
options.rationale: Reaches the correct conclusion but doesn't justify it — a stronger answer explains specifically why each matrix serves a different governance or technical purpose, rather than simply asserting both should be retained.

options.action: Recommend keeping both: the Data Entity/Business Function Matrix supports assigning data ownership to organizations and enabling data governance programs at the business-function level (e.g., establishing data stewards). The Application/Data Matrix supports understanding which specific applications technically create, read, update, and delete data entities — critical for migration scoping and technical dependency analysis. These serve distinct governance and technical purposes rather than duplicating each other.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly distinguishes the business-governance purpose of one matrix from the technical-dependency purpose of the other, explaining why both remain valuable rather than redundant.

options.action: Suggest merging the two matrices into a single combined matrix covering both business functions and applications together against data entities.
options.rationale: Creates an overly complex, harder-to-use artifact — combining two matrices with genuinely different audiences and purposes (business governance vs. technical dependency mapping) into one matrix makes it less clear and useful for either audience, rather than preserving the distinct value each currently provides.

lessonTitle: Phase D — Technology Architecture
sourceRef: C220-Part1e §9.3.10 — sequencing guidance: implement difficult activities after easier ones absent compelling reasons
scenario: While sequencing Technology Architecture work packages for the Roadmap, a planning team proposes tackling the single most technically difficult component first, arguing: "Let's get the hardest part done immediately while the team is fresh and motivated." No specific business or technical reason is given for this particular difficult component needing to go first.

options.action: Support the plan — starting with the most difficult activity while morale is high is generally sound project management, regardless of the specific circumstances.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard's specific sequencing guidance. It states that difficult activities should be identified and, unless there are compelling reasons otherwise, implemented after other activities that most easily deliver missing capability — team motivation alone doesn't constitute the kind of compelling reason this guidance calls for.

options.action: Push back on the sequencing, but only citing general risk-management best practice rather than the Standard's specific guidance on this point.
options.rationale: Reaches a reasonable objection but doesn't ground it in the Standard's specific sequencing principle — citing the explicit "implement difficult activities after easier ones absent compelling reasons" guidance gives the team clear authority for reconsidering the plan.

options.action: Push back, citing the Standard's specific guidance: difficult activities should generally be implemented after other activities that most easily deliver missing capability, unless there are compelling reasons to do otherwise. Ask whether there's a compelling reason (e.g., a hard dependency or a critical business driver) for tackling this particular difficult component first — if not, recommend sequencing it later, after activities that deliver capability more readily.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly cites the Standard's specific sequencing principle and asks the right diagnostic question (is there a compelling reason?) rather than either accepting or rejecting the proposal outright.

options.action: Insist that difficult activities must always be scheduled last in every case, with no exceptions ever permitted regardless of circumstances.
options.rationale: Overstates the guidance as an absolute rule. The Standard's language is 'unless there are compelling reasons' — it explicitly allows for exceptions when genuinely justified, rather than treating 'difficult last' as an inviolable rule with zero flexibility.

lessonTitle: Phase D — Technology Architecture
sourceRef: C220-Part1e §8.3.5 — Technology Roadmap as "raw material" for the consolidated cross-discipline roadmap in Phase E
scenario: Upon completing Phase D gap analysis, a Technology Architect produces a detailed Technology Roadmap and declares: "This is now the official Architecture Roadmap for the programme — Phase E will just need to formally adopt it."

options.action: Agree — the Phase D Technology Roadmap becomes the official Architecture Roadmap once Phase E formally adopts it as-is.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard directly. It describes the initial Technology Architecture roadmap as raw material to support more detailed definition of a consolidated, cross-discipline roadmap within Phase E — not as something Phase E simply adopts wholesale; Phase E must integrate it with Business, Data, and Application Architecture gap analysis results too.

options.action: Disagree, and say Phase E needs to do 'more work' on it, without specifying that Business, Data, and Application roadmap components must also be integrated.
options.rationale: Correctly senses the Technology Roadmap isn't final but doesn't explain what specifically Phase E must add — a stronger answer identifies that the other three domains' candidate roadmap components need to be consolidated alongside the Technology Roadmap.

options.action: Disagree: the Standard describes the Phase D Technology Roadmap as raw material supporting a more detailed, consolidated, cross-discipline roadmap developed within Phase E — not a document Phase E simply adopts. Phase E must integrate this Technology Roadmap with the candidate roadmap components from Business Architecture (Phase B) and Data/Application Architecture (Phase C) into one genuinely consolidated Architecture Roadmap.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly characterizes the Technology Roadmap's actual status (raw material, not final) and explains what Phase E's consolidation work specifically involves.

options.action: Suggest the Technology Roadmap should be discarded entirely and Phase E should start the roadmap-building process completely from scratch.
options.rationale: Discards valuable work unnecessarily — the Technology Roadmap is explicitly described as raw material to be used in Phase E's consolidation, not material to be thrown away; the issue is that it isn't yet the final Architecture Roadmap, not that it has no value at all.

lessonTitle: Phase D — Technology Architecture
scenario: A Phase D team finalizes the Target Technology Architecture and prepares to move to Phase E without checking whether this Technology Architecture affects any other projects currently running elsewhere in the organization.

options.action: Proceed directly to Phase E — since the Target Technology Architecture for this engagement is finalized, checking other unrelated projects is unnecessary additional work.
options.rationale: Skips a defined Phase D step. Resolving impacts across the Architecture Landscape specifically requires examining whether this Technology Architecture creates impacts on pre-existing architectures, and whether it impacts or will be impacted by other projects — whether planned or currently in progress — before considering the phase complete.

options.action: Suggest checking for impacts on other projects, but treat it as an optional courtesy check rather than a required step of the phase.
options.rationale: Reaches a reasonable practical instinct but understates its status — resolving impacts across the Architecture Landscape is a specifically defined Phase D step, not an optional courtesy to extend to other teams if time allows.

options.action: Recommend completing the defined Phase D step of resolving impacts across the Architecture Landscape before proceeding: specifically checking whether this Technology Architecture impacts other projects (planned or in progress), whether it will be impacted by them, and whether there are opportunities to leverage this work elsewhere in the organization — this is a required part of finalizing Phase D, not an optional add-on.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly identifies this as a specifically defined, required Phase D step and names the actual questions it involves, rather than treating it as optional.

options.action: Suggest this check only matters for large, enterprise-wide programmes, and can be safely skipped for smaller, more contained engagements.
options.rationale: Introduces an unsupported scale-based exception — the Standard's guidance to resolve impacts across the Architecture Landscape doesn't include a size threshold; even smaller engagements can have unexpected impacts on other in-progress or planned work that are worth checking.

lessonTitle: Phase D — Technology Architecture
scenario: A Phase D architect is finalizing building block selections and says: "Since we're on a tight deadline, let's skip re-using anything from the Architecture Repository's reference models and just build all Technology Building Blocks fresh, tailored precisely to this project."

options.action: Support building everything fresh — a tight deadline justifies bypassing existing reference models in favor of custom-building all technology building blocks from scratch.
options.rationale: Works against both the deadline pressure and the Standard's approach. Finalizing the Technology Architecture specifically involves selecting standards for building blocks while re-using as much as possible from reference models already selected in the Architecture Repository — building everything fresh typically takes longer, not less time, than leveraging existing, proven models.

options.action: Push back on building everything fresh, but without explaining that re-use is specifically part of the Standard's finalization guidance rather than just generally good practice.
options.rationale: Reaches a reasonable objection but doesn't ground it in the specific finalization step — the Standard specifically directs re-using reference models from the Architecture Repository as part of finalizing the Technology Architecture, not just as generic good practice worth considering.

options.action: Push back: finalizing the Technology Architecture specifically involves selecting standards for each building block while re-using as much as possible from reference models already available in the Architecture Repository. Given the tight deadline, re-use is likely to save time compared to building everything fresh, not cost it — recommend checking the Repository for applicable reference models before committing to custom-building every component.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly cites the Standard's specific re-use guidance for finalizing Technology Architecture, and reframes the deadline pressure as an argument for re-use rather than against it.

options.action: Suggest re-use should only be considered after the deadline has already passed and can be retrofitted later if time allows.
options.rationale: Defers a step that's meant to happen as part of finalizing the Technology Architecture itself, not as a post-deadline retrofit — re-using reference models from the Repository is specifically part of how building blocks are finalized in Phase D, and doing it now is more efficient than building fresh and reconciling with reference models afterward.

lessonTitle: Phases E & F — Opportunities & Solutions, and Migration Planning
sourceRef: C220-Part1e §9.1 — Phase E's three objectives
scenario: A Phase E team believes their only job is to produce the Architecture Roadmap, and once that's drafted, declares the phase complete and ready for Phase F.

options.action: Confirm Phase E is complete — producing the Architecture Roadmap is the sole objective of the phase.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard directly. Phase E has three objectives: generating the initial complete Architecture Roadmap; determining whether an incremental approach is needed and identifying Transition Architectures if so; and defining the overall Solution Building Blocks (SBBs) to finalize the Target Architecture based on the ABBs. Only the first has been addressed.

options.action: Point out something is missing, without naming the other two specific objectives (Transition Architectures determination, and SBB definition).
options.rationale: Correctly senses incompleteness but doesn't specify what's actually missing — a stronger answer names both remaining objectives explicitly.

options.action: Point out that Phase E has three objectives, not one: alongside the Architecture Roadmap, the team must also determine whether an incremental approach is required (and if so, identify Transition Architectures delivering continuous business value), and define the overall Solution Building Blocks needed to finalize the Target Architecture based on the ABBs already defined. None of this has been addressed yet.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly names all three Phase E objectives and identifies precisely which two remain unaddressed before the phase can be considered complete.

options.action: Suggest the Transition Architecture and SBB work can simply be deferred to Phase F instead of completed within Phase E.
options.rationale: Misplaces the responsibility — determining Transition Architectures and defining SBBs are explicitly Phase E objectives; Phase F's role is to finalize the Architecture Roadmap and Implementation and Migration Plan building on Phase E's completed work, not to perform Phase E's own objectives on its behalf.

lessonTitle: Phases E & F — Opportunities & Solutions, and Migration Planning
sourceRef: C220-Part1e §10.1 — Phase F's three objectives
scenario: A Phase F team finalizes a detailed Implementation and Migration Plan showing costs, timelines, and resources, and considers Phase F complete — without checking whether the plan aligns with any of the organization's other ongoing change initiatives, and without formally confirming stakeholders understand the business value of each work package.

options.action: Confirm Phase F is complete — finalizing the detailed Implementation and Migration Plan satisfies the entirety of what Phase F requires.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard directly. Phase F has three objectives: finalizing the Architecture Roadmap and Implementation and Migration Plan; ensuring the Plan is coordinated with the enterprise's overall change portfolio; and ensuring key stakeholders understand the business value and cost of work packages and Transition Architectures. Only the first has been completed.

options.action: Point out something is missing, without naming the two remaining objectives (portfolio coordination and stakeholder understanding of business value/cost).
options.rationale: Correctly identifies incompleteness but doesn't specify what's missing — naming both remaining objectives would make the gap actionable rather than just noted.

options.action: Point out that Phase F has three objectives, not one: alongside finalizing the plan, the team must also ensure it's coordinated with the enterprise's overall approach to managing and implementing change across its change portfolio, and ensure key stakeholders genuinely understand the business value and cost of each work package and Transition Architecture. Neither has been confirmed yet.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly names all three Phase F objectives and identifies exactly which two remain unaddressed, showing the phase isn't yet complete.

options.action: Suggest stakeholder understanding of business value is a Phase A concern, already addressed earlier, and doesn't need to be revisited in Phase F.
options.rationale: Misunderstands the objective's scope — while Phase A defines initial value propositions and KPIs, Phase F specifically requires ensuring stakeholders understand the business value and cost of the now-finalized work packages and Transition Architectures at this later stage of detail, not simply relying on earlier, higher-level Phase A discussions.

lessonTitle: Phases E & F — Opportunities & Solutions, and Migration Planning
scenario: A Phase E team identifies four Transition Architectures and schedules them at exactly six-month intervals each, arguing: "Consistent, uniform spacing makes the roadmap easier to communicate and manage."

options.action: Support the uniform six-month spacing — consistent intervals between Transition Architectures are a requirement for a well-formed Architecture Roadmap.
options.rationale: Introduces a constraint the Standard doesn't require. It explicitly notes the time-span between successive Transition Architectures does not have to be of uniform duration — spacing should instead be driven by what each Transition Architecture is designed to deliver and the dependencies involved, not forced into equal intervals for communication convenience.

options.action: Disagree with forcing uniform spacing, but without citing that the Standard explicitly states intervals need not be uniform.
options.rationale: Reaches a reasonable conclusion but doesn't ground it in the Standard's specific guidance — citing the explicit statement that intervals don't need to be uniform gives the team clear authority to sequence based on actual content and dependencies instead.

options.action: Disagree: the Standard explicitly states the time-span between successive Transition Architectures does not have to be of uniform duration. Spacing should instead be driven by what each Transition Architecture needs to deliver, dependencies between work packages, and the enterprise's capacity for absorbing change — not forced into equal intervals purely for communication simplicity, which risks either rushing complex transitions or unnecessarily delaying simple ones.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly cites the Standard's explicit permission for non-uniform spacing and explains why forcing uniformity risks poor sequencing decisions.

options.action: Suggest the number of Transition Architectures should be reduced to exactly two, since fewer transitions are always easier to manage regardless of spacing.
options.rationale: Introduces an unrelated and unsupported constraint — the appropriate number of Transition Architectures depends on the complexity of the gap between Baseline and Target and the enterprise's change capacity, not a fixed preference for fewer transitions regardless of what's actually needed to deliver incremental business value.

lessonTitle: Phases E & F — Opportunities & Solutions, and Migration Planning
scenario: A Phase F team is deciding how to sequence application system implementations and proposes: "Let's just implement all applications simultaneously in one big-bang go-live, since that avoids the complexity of managing multiple sequential releases."

options.action: Support the big-bang approach — implementing all applications simultaneously avoids sequencing complexity and is therefore the simpler choice.
options.rationale: Ignores the dependency-driven logic the Standard describes for migration planning, such as a data-driven sequence where application systems that create data are implemented before applications that process that data. A big-bang approach ignoring these dependencies risks systems going live without the data or upstream components they depend on being ready.

options.action: Push back on the big-bang approach, but without explaining the specific dependency-driven sequencing logic (e.g., data-creating systems before data-processing systems) that the Standard describes.
options.rationale: Reaches a reasonable objection but doesn't explain the underlying principle — a stronger answer would specifically reference dependency and lifecycle considerations between systems, not just a general preference for phased delivery.

options.action: Push back: migration planning should consider dependency-driven sequencing approaches, such as a data-driven sequence where application systems that create data are implemented before applications that process that data. A clear understanding of the dependencies and lifecycle of in-place Solution Building Blocks is required for an effective Implementation and Migration Plan — a big-bang approach risks violating these dependencies by going live with downstream systems before their upstream data sources are ready.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly cites the Standard's specific dependency-sequencing guidance and explains precisely why ignoring it in a big-bang approach creates real implementation risk.

options.action: Suggest sequencing should be based purely on which applications are cheapest to implement, regardless of data or functional dependencies between them.
options.rationale: Replaces one flawed sequencing logic (big-bang, ignoring dependencies) with another equally flawed one — cost alone, without regard to data creation/processing dependencies or SBB lifecycle considerations, risks the same kind of implementation failure the Standard's dependency-based guidance is meant to prevent.

lessonTitle: Phases G & H — Implementation Governance and Architecture Change Management
sourceRef: C220-Part1e §12.5 — three change categories (Simplification/Incremental/Re-architecting) and their investment drivers
scenario: Three change requests arrive in the same week: CR-1 proposes retiring a redundant legacy interface to cut infrastructure costs. CR-2 proposes adding an AI-powered upsell feature to an existing e-commerce platform, using its current architecture. CR-3 proposes entering an entirely new business line requiring new capabilities never before supported by the enterprise. A change manager says: "These all look similar to me — let's just log them all as 'incremental changes' and handle them the same way."

options.action: Agree — since all three are change requests of some kind, classifying them uniformly as incremental changes is a reasonable simplification.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard's specific three-way classification. Simplification changes are driven by a requirement to reduce investment (CR-1 fits here); incremental changes are driven by deriving additional value from existing investment (CR-2 fits here); re-architecting changes are driven by a requirement to increase investment to create new value (CR-3 fits here) — treating all three identically misses genuinely different governance and investment implications.

options.action: Disagree, and say the three requests seem different, without applying the Standard's specific investment-driven classification test to each one.
options.rationale: Correctly senses a distinction but doesn't apply the actual test — the Standard's specific framing (reduce investment vs. derive value from existing investment vs. increase investment for new value) gives a precise way to classify each request rather than a vague sense that they differ.

options.action: Disagree, and classify each using the Standard's specific test: CR-1 (retiring a redundant interface to cut costs) is a simplification change, driven by reducing investment. CR-2 (adding a feature using existing architecture) is an incremental change, driven by deriving additional value from existing investment. CR-3 (an entirely new business line requiring new capabilities) is a re-architecting change, driven by increasing investment to create new value — requiring the full architecture development cycle again.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly applies the Standard's specific investment-driven classification test to each of the three requests, showing why they require different governance treatment rather than uniform handling.

options.action: Suggest classifying all three as re-architecting changes, to be safe, since this ensures maximum governance rigor is applied to every request.
options.rationale: Over-applies rigor disproportionately — treating a simple cost-reduction change (CR-1) as requiring the full architecture development cycle again is unnecessarily heavy-handed and inconsistent with the Standard's own three-tier classification, which exists precisely to right-size governance effort to the nature of the change.

lessonTitle: Phases G & H — Implementation Governance and Architecture Change Management
sourceRef: C220-Part1e §11.5 — Phase G ensures compliance not only by implementation projects but by other ongoing projects
scenario: During Phase G, the governance team reviews the specific implementation project delivering the Target Architecture and confirms full compliance. A team member says: "Our Phase G compliance review is complete — we've checked the one project actually implementing this architecture."

options.action: Confirm the review is complete — checking compliance of the specific implementation project delivering this Target Architecture satisfies Phase G's compliance requirement.
options.rationale: Contradicts the Standard directly. It specifically states that ensuring compliance with the defined architecture is a key aspect of Phase G not only for implementation projects delivering this architecture, but also for other ongoing projects within the enterprise that might be affected by or need to align with it.

options.action: Disagree, and say other projects should probably be checked too, without specifying this is an explicit part of the Standard's Phase G compliance scope.
options.rationale: Reaches a reasonable conclusion but doesn't ground it — citing the Standard's explicit statement that compliance review extends to other ongoing projects gives the team clear authority for broadening the review, rather than a vague sense that more checking might be prudent.

options.action: Disagree: the Standard explicitly states that ensuring compliance is a key aspect of Phase G not only for the implementation projects delivering this architecture, but also for other ongoing projects within the enterprise. Recommend identifying any other currently active projects that may be affected by or should conform to this architecture, and including them in the compliance review before considering it complete.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly cites the Standard's explicit scope for Phase G compliance review and recommends the specific action needed (identify and review other affected ongoing projects).

options.action: Suggest expanding the review to check literally every project across the entire enterprise, regardless of any plausible connection to this architecture.
options.rationale: Overcorrects into an unbounded scope — the Standard's guidance is about other ongoing projects relevant to or potentially affected by this specific architecture, not an indiscriminate review of every unrelated project in the enterprise regardless of connection.

lessonTitle: Phases G & H — Implementation Governance and Architecture Change Management
scenario: A Phase H team notices a steady decline in usage of a core business capability that the Enterprise Architecture was designed to support several years ago. One team member says: "As long as the architecture documentation is technically still accurate and up to date, there's nothing for Phase H to act on here."

options.action: Agree — Phase H's role is limited to keeping documentation technically accurate; declining business usage of a supported capability isn't something Phase H needs to act on if the documents are current.
options.rationale: Misses a core purpose of Phase H. Monitoring business growth and decline is described as a critical aspect of this phase — architectures can remain technically well-documented while no longer serving the actual needs of the business, which is exactly the kind of drift Phase H exists to catch, not just document accuracy in isolation.

options.action: Disagree, and say declining usage 'seems worth investigating,' without connecting this to Phase H's specific monitoring responsibility.
options.rationale: Reaches a reasonable instinct but doesn't tie it to the Standard's stated purpose — a stronger answer explicitly identifies monitoring business growth and decline as a defined Phase H responsibility, not just a generally sensible thing to look into.

options.action: Disagree: monitoring business growth and decline is described as a critical aspect of Phase H, precisely because an architecture may remain technically accurate while no longer meeting the needs of today's or tomorrow's enterprise. Recommend investigating why usage of this capability is declining — the underlying solutions or business processes may need updating even if the architecture description itself hasn't changed.
options.rationale: Best answer — correctly identifies monitoring business growth/decline as a specific, named Phase H responsibility and explains why technical documentation accuracy alone doesn't satisfy it.

options.action: Suggest the declining usage should be escalated directly to Phase B for a completely new Business Architecture cycle, without further investigation in Phase H first.
options.rationale: Skips ahead prematurely — Phase H's role is to monitor, investigate, and determine whether a new architecture evolution cycle is warranted; jumping straight to initiating a new Phase B cycle without first understanding the cause of the decline bypasses the classification and evaluation Phase H is meant to perform.

lessonTitle: Phases G & H — Implementation Governance and Architecture Change Management
scenario: A Phase G team documents an Architecture Contract but doesn't obtain signatures from all developing organizations involved, reasoning: "The lead development team has signed off, and that should be sufficient to proceed."

options.action: Agree — a signature from the lead development team alone is sufficient to consider the Architecture Contract properly executed.
options.rationale: Misses a specific requirement in documenting the Architecture Contract. This step specifically involves obtaining signatures from all developing organizations and the sponsoring organization — not just the lead developer — since the Contract is a joint agreement establishing shared accountability for deliverables, quality, and fitness-for-purpose across all parties involved.
